speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture some time ago announced federal assistance of $450 million to Canadian grain and oilseed producers to help address the projected income shortfall caused by unfair foreign export subsidies. I congratulate the minister on his decision to turn these moneys over to the provinces so that each province can devise eligibility and delivery criteria that will best address the needs of its producers. Putting the province in charge of distribution should reduce the time delays inherent in national ad hoc programs.
Some $237 million of this federal money will go to Saskatchewan for distribution to producers along with whatever additional funds the province of Saskatchewan is prepared to put up. This assistance is further tangible evidence of this government's ongoing commitment to Canadian and Saskatchewan producers.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the government finally released the initial prices of Ontario wheat, affecting 18,000 producers. In spite of numerous requests from the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board, the government should recognize its responsibilities in the international trade war which threatens to destroy Canadian
agriculture and ensure an initial price for all Ontario wheat of $130 a tonne. The government has refused.
The government eliminated the at and east transportation program, the Advance Payments for Crops Program, and now the government has set the initial price at $20 to $30 per tonne below the farmers' actual cost of production. These initial low prices cannot be justified by the market when world stocks are at historic lows. An initial price for Ontario white winter wheat of $115 a tonne is unacceptable. This is a drop of $15 a tonne, a drop of 11.5 per cent.
I call on the government to respond to the international trade war, which has lowered grain prices by $20 to $30 a tonne, by implementing an export program for Canada's producers and restore the two-price wheat policy to ensure an equitable return for Canada's producers.

Mr. Speaker, in the printing industry today, space-age satellite technology allows typesetting and film to be prepared offshore, usually in Pacific Rim countries, and then to be transmitted to Canada by satellite. Before the advent of this technology, when that work entered Canada, it was subject to duty. Today it is not. This means pre-press shops in Canada compete with firms in Hong Kong and Taiwan with wage scales two-thirds lower than ours. This is a clear case of public policy not keeping up with technology.
As a result of the free trade agreement, the hyper competitive Canadian print market has been opened to giant U.S. printing firms, squeezing the Canadian industry and limiting its ability to modernize. As well, a 25 per cent drop in Canadian print exports is a direct result of this government's high interest rate policy.
I urge the government to move to ensure this critical part of the communication industry remains healthy and viable.

May 30, 1990

Mr. Speaker, Alice Linden of London, Ontario, says she does not want to tell her great-grandchildren she stood by in 1990 and did nothing to stop Canada from breaking up.
So, at noon today in London, she organized her own rally to send a message of unity to the people of Canada. In so doing, she awakened the sleeping giant in our community. Hundreds of Londoners, including John King and the students from Mountsfield Public School, used their lunch hour to stand up and be counted. Their message was simple. With hand lettered signs, and dressed in red and white, these people reached out in support and understanding to our neighbours in Quebec.
The people of London, in the heart of English Canada, want the rest of Canada to know that they will not sit quietly and allow a noisy minority to split the country we love. Alice and people like her are the silent majority in our country. With them, a powerful momentum is building in the hamlets, villages, towns and cities across our great land. It begs to be heard before it is too late. Keep Canada together. Gordons le Canada uni.
Congratulations, Alice. I call upon the silent majority of Canadians to break their silence and join her fight.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Printing Industries Association is meeting this week in Ottawa. Our printing industry employs 60,000 Canadians through more than 3,000 establishments, almost all of them Canadian-owned small businesses. Its sales are nearly $2 billion per year.
In 1989, the first year under free trade, our printing imports were up 20 per cent, exports were down 25 per cent, and Canada's trade deficit in printed materials skyrocketed 142 per cent.
One thousand Canadian printers lost their jobs last year. This sorry performance is a result of Tory government policies, high interest rates, a high dollar and a free
trade deal that permits Americans to unfairly discriminate against our Canadian printers. When will the Government of Canada stand up for Canada's printers? When will the Government of Canada stand up for Canada's businesses? When will it stand up for Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I have a copy of CN inter-office correspondence dated February 22,1990, sent by Mr. Bourgeois, Director of Quebec City operations, to Mr. Boucher, Regional Director in Montreal, concerning two different scenarios for putting the Chapais subdivision, between Franquet and Chapais, back in service.
The first scenario would be to accommodate traffic if necessary-which implies that the section will be strictly used as an emergency detour-and the second, to put back into circulation a certain volume of traffic as specified in another memo.
In concluding, Mr. Bourgeois added the following: "If, as expected, we plan to put the section back into service, to be used only if necessary".
Mr. Speaker, once again, the President of CN and the big bosses in Quebec City and Montreal have blithely ignored the ruling by the National Transportation Agency of Canada on January 31, 1990, as well as CN workers and the various economic partners in Abitibi.

Mr. Speaker, the low value placed on Canada's forests by provincial governments has led to wasted resources and a poor return to Canadians. A classic example is the strong demand in the United States for recycled newsprint. Because of the ready access to under-priced trees, pulp mills in Canada produce almost entirely virgin pulp and paper, much of it for U.S. markets.
May 30, 1990

At a time when existing mills should be adding de-inking facilities to recycle newsprint and paper, and when new mills should be designing in recycling capacity, we see inaction.
The Canadian forest barons clearly intend to hand over the major recycling market to U.S. firms and to continue gobbling Canadian forests.
The former Minister of the Environment pointed out that 80 million trees, the entire annual cut of the province of Ontario, could be saved by setting recycling standards in Canada to that of Japan. We should not be filling our landfills with recyclable paper. Paper fibre can be recycled seven times, not once.
Forty per cent of the marine pollution in Canada is from pulp mills. It is time they cleaned up, reduced their cut and waste, and recycled their product. Canada needs law on recycling.

Mr. Speaker, I recently had occasion to go through Pearson International Airport's Terminal II which is presently undergoing renovations. I noticed that the terminal was sporting many cartoons and murals and had pamphlets with cartoon characters drawn by American Mad Magazine artist Don Martin.
Upon investigation it was discovered that the art was commissioned by Air Canada, a Crown corporation. While the characters are highly amusing, I could not understand why Air Canada would choose an American over a Canadian artist. There is a happy ending to this. Further investigation found that while the copyrighted figures belong to artist Don Martin, the layout and design was done by Canadian artists. In fact, I discovered that Air Canada has the largest private art bank in Canada and they are very involved in promoting young Canadian artists.
I would like to commend Air Canada on their role for the enhancement and the status of the Canadian artist.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to welcome the
visit of Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and his wife Raisa to Canada. They have certainly impressed Canadians and we warmly wish this man of peace every success.
I would also like to take this time to urge our government to support President Gorbachev's efforts of reform. But, to do so, Canada must first increase its diplomatic presence in the Soviet Union.
Mr. Speaker, the opening of a new Canadian consulate in Kiev has been delayed. Canada should have a consulate in Leningrad. Our Moscow embassy is seriously understaffed. Stronger ties between the Soviet Union and Canada are impossible without a greater Canadian presence in the Soviet Union, including greater Canadian expertise in Soviet languages and Soviet affairs. Among other faults, the lack of Canadian personnel in the Soviet Union makes it unnecessarily difficult for those wishing to emigrate from the Soviet Union to Canada. We in the Liberal party believe in supporting greater Canadian-Soviet relations in areas such as economy, agriculture, Arctic protection, and the environment.
Therefore I urge the government to take the opportunity of Mr. Gorbachev's visit to secure Soviet co-operation, to proceed immediately with the opening of new Canadian consulates in the Soviet Union, and to increase the Canadian presence in our existing embassy in Moscow.

Mr. Speaker, we have the honour and the privilege of receiving in Canada a great statesman, the President of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, Mr. Mikhail Gorbachev, the man who ended the cold war.
Thanks to wide-ranging reforms that are taking place in Eastern Europe, a new era of liberalization, unification and openness is bom.
Canada has its place in the history of this process. Last February, it hosted the first "Open Skies" conference, attended by foreign affairs ministers of the 23 NATO And Warsaw Pact countries.

May 30, 1990
Oral Questions
During our Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union last November, 14 bilateral agreements were signed, on subjects ranging from international relations in the Arctic to the environment and trade.
President Gorbachev's visit to Canada will no doubt be an important event in the history of Soviet-Canadian relations. We must now look to the future and consider the major issues.
Mr. Speaker, once again, Canada and our Prime Minister are playing a leading role in achieving more peaceful relations between countries the world over.

Mr. Speaker, the government's commitment to the environment does not stand the test. Salisbury, a community in my riding, is very disappointed at the lack of support it received from the government when it tried to participate in federal government environmental programs. Schools in my area are in need of federal funds to support their recycling projects.

Their students are not trying to collect money to pay for trips or the prom. These students are concerned about the environment. All they want is a small amount of money to help them carry out their project.

We are encouraging people to get involved, but we are not delivering at the other end. We are building support and commitment, but we cannot deliver at the program level. We have top down programs rather than bottom up. Without effective programs we will ultimately lose the support of the people and then we will lose our environment.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of most people responsible for economic policy, I will direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister whoever he or she may be.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Exporters Association both agree that the government's high interest rate policy as well as the exchange rate policy are creating a lot of problems for exporters in the country. As a matter of fact it is disastrous for the manufacturing sector particularly.
Is the government now prepared to listen to the manufacturing sector, the Canadian premiers, the Canadian Labour Congress, and consumers and change the disastrous monetary policy that is wrecking our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks about the level of the dollar and our manufacturing
sector.
I think he knows that the World Economic Forum judged Canada the fourth most productive economy in the world in 1988. The study to which he is making reference was done in 1988. This was before the government was able to bring in the free trade agreement, which makes our manufacturing sector more competitive. It was also before we were able to bring legislation before the House to get rid of the manufacturers' sales tax, which is very important to the manufacturing sector.
More important, we have for example Chrysler's $400 million investment. We have Stelco expanding. We have the forest products industry expanding. We have CATO Industries expanding and a number of high-tech firms. There are endless stories of manufacturing investment increasing.
However, the most important point for the hon. member to remember is that recently we have some pressures on labour costs. They are starting to rise. This we must deal with, and that we are doing.
May 30, 1990

Mr. Speaker, obviously the minister is not aware that as recently as this week the Canadian Exporters Association and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association both indicated that they are in a very precarious position as a result of the high dollar policy of this government.
There are studies that indicate we are at a 40-year low in terms of our competitiveness in the U.S. market. I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister or whoever is speaking for the government on economic matters today a question.
Do they not understand the depth of the problem being articulated by the leading Canadian business spokespeople in this country? Do they not recognize that they have to change their high interest, high dollar policy, or Canadian exports are going to face a disastrous situation from which they will not recover for many years, if ever?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that the way to be competitive is to control costs. Two absolutely essential ways to control costs is to make sure that labour costs are reasonable and that inflationary pressures in the country do not increase.
The two biggest threats we have to the structure of costs in the manufacturing industry are inflationary pressures that come from excess demands and excess credit. The Bank of Canada's efforts on the monetary side are helping with that. However, more important, we have a fiscal policy which has been responsible and which is also doing its bit to ensure costs are kept in line. This we must do. To lower the dollar would simply increase enormously input costs, especially for the manufacturing sector. That is not the way to go.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear the minister fails to understand what all Canadians are trying to tell him. The budget brought down by the Minister of Finance on February 20 projected a bank rate of 11.1 per cent. The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce tells us this is out of the question. In fact, people have been saying this ever since the budget was brought down.
My question for the Acting Prime Minister is this: Considering that the bank rate will not be 11.1 per cent
Oral Questions
this year, and considering that our expenditures will be at least $2 billion more than was estimated in the Budget, will the government bring down a new Budget that reflects the current economic situation in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that the Minister of Finance has said no to that proposition. He has also made it clear that income tax revenues are flowing a little better than expected. That helps to balance the pessimistic comments he made about interest rate costs.
However, more important, to artificially take the dollar or to take interest rates and lower them would simply chase investment out of Canada and increase enormously the cost of manufacturing inputs and all sorts of imports we get from other countries. This would simply lead to the kind of spiral we had in 1981-1982 when interest rates were 22 per cent and 23 per cent and inflation was running at 14 per cent and 15 per cent. This we do not want, and this is what we are fighting.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister for International Trade, if there is one in the House. A report by the Canadian Printing Industries Association, published a year after the free trade agreement with the United States came into force, indicates there has been a 25 per cent drop in exports. Could the Acting Minister for International Trade inform the House what the government intends to do to stop a process that threatens the very existence of the printing industry in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

The government is trying to moderate inflation and to keep the cost of inputs and imports down. A large part of the imports in the printing industry come from offshore. We are trying to moderate inflation, to make sure those costs do not go up, and to make sure the price of imports

May 30, 1990

do not go up. However, above all, by removing the manufacturers' sales tax, by removing the 13.5 per cent tax and putting in its place a tax which is virtually instantly rebated through input tax credit, is good news for that industry. I hope the hon. member will support us in that.

Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the minister says, free trade, the high dollar, the elimination of postal subsidy, and the GST are badly hurting the Canadian printing industry.
Maybe the minister should read the report from the Canadian printing industry so that he will realize the damage they are doing to the industry.
My question to the minister is very simple. Why does the government want to destroy the printing industry in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

Mr. Speaker, if one takes the conclusions at which the hon. member has just invited the House to arrive with him, that first we should have a lower dollar which would increase the cost of machinery for the printing industry enormously, and if he wants to reinstate all the tariffs that existed before free trade and make sure we could not lower tariffs, that would increase the cost to the printing industry enormously.
If he is also arguing that he does not want the industry to look globally and in a continental sense, then he is asking for the very opposite of what this industry is asking for. It wants to be competitive, it wants a chance at world markets, and it wants low cost imports.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister or whoever is responsible for external affairs today.
Many Canadians have shown strong support for the democratic aspirations of the Baltic nations and for a peaceful resolution to the present crisis in that part of the world.
Will the Acting Prime Minister assure us that it has been made clear to Mr. Gorbachev that Canadians know
his economic blockade of Lithuania runs contrary to his earlier assurances of no forceful intervention?
Given the conciliatory offers of compromise recently made by the Baltic negotiators, will the Canadian government urge Mr. Gorbachev to suspend the economic boycott of Lithuania and, particularly, the blockade of medical supplies which is now reaching catastrophic dimensions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is aware of our policy, which has been consistent in this House, from statements made on several occasions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. She knows perfectly well that our position remains the same. We have confirmed our position of non-recognition, de jure, of Lithuania's annexation by the Soviet Union. We urged the Soviet authorities to show moderation, and we condemned their blockade of Lithuania. We emphasized the need for dialogue, and that is certainly the message that has been transmitted to the authorities during their visit. We still think that dialogue and moderation are the best way to deal with this kind of conflict.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is very brief.
Would the government be willing to provide advice and assistance to the Lithuanian Canadian community and others in Canada who are trying to find a way to get much needed medical supplies into Lithuania?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are of course very concerned about the situation in Lithuania, and we can assure Canadians that, should certain groups wish to send medical equipment or supplies to Lithuania, we would be willing to consider, assist and support this kind of operation. At the present time, however, we have not received any requests from official authorities in that country. We are prepared to consider any assistance offered by Canadian authorities or the Canadian public.
May 30, 1990

Mr. Speaker, the government knows that the Baltic crisis should be resolved within the framework of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
The Baltic republics will be seeking observer participant status at the upcoming meeting on the human dimension in Copenhagen. Will the Acting Prime Minister give us her assurance that Canada will support that request?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows perfectly well that the President of the Soviet Union is still in Canada and that the talks are not over yet. I am sure that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs returns to the House, he will be happy to inform the House about the discussions that took place and various representations the Government of Canada has made to the Soviet authorities.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the minister who today answers for fisheries. The free trade panel has decided against Canada, a decision which will cost Canadian lobster fishermen $30 million. Will the minister now specify what financial assistance will be made available to Atlantic lobster fishermen to get them through this crisis?

Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, this is a trade question and the last time I looked lobsters were a commodity that this country trades.
On the question of the loss of trade through the decision made by the panel, I said yesterday that this gives us a 90-day-period for industry, labour and governments to get together to see what they can put together.
Oral Questions
The most important fact that this hon. member should be aware of is that we are promoting in a massive way the smaller lobsters in other countries as well as the larger lobsters in the United States, so much so that the original estimate of $30 million will certainly not turn out to be accurate. The promotional campaign is working very well. In fact, in recent months industry and the provinces have made a concerted effort to reduce inventories from $20 million in January to about $4.7 million. So we are having great luck with our promotion campaign.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. The promotional package announced last week is not enough. Promotion will only sell lobsters bought from fishermen at $1.25 a pound. This is not good enough if they are forced out of business by this year's low prices.
Therefore, will the minister immediately commit his government to providing a price package to help lobster fishermen now?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member will find this list of what the minister has committed long, but it is very important.
First, External Affairs and International Trade have identified lobsters to Canadian posts as priority fishing market items for this year. We have also encouraged the formation of the Canadian Atlantic Lobster Promotion Association for generic image and quality promotion. We have undertaken a world-wide survey of markets through Canadian posts with results that are soon to be released. We are working with the industry, the provinces and the associations directly to make officials aware of the many opportunities, opportunities which this country has not taken proper advantage of in the past to promote this product, not simply through grocery stores and restaurants but through trade fairs and other contexts.
We believe not just in subsidizing and subsidizing but in promoting, and it is working.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. The major environmental scourge in the Great Lakes is the zebra mussel, a parasite imported from Europe. It has already totally infested Lake Erie and Lake St. Clair,

May 30, 1990
Oral Questions
almost all of Lake Ontario, and it is now showing signs in Lake Huron and Lake Superior. It creates havoc for industry and for governmental agencies, especially municipalities.
The American government is committing $37.5 million to control it. Ontario Hydro is spending over $10 million and we do not know how much Ford is spending to correct it. Industries like Ford are spending millions. The only institution not doing anything effectively is this government.
Will the minister commit the necessary funds today to control the zebra mussel spread in the Great Lakes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which the hon. member raises is very important. I want to reassure him by indicating that this government is working in close co-operation with the Ontario government, with American counterparts, with Great Lakes authorities and with the universities.
There are currently in place some 26 research projects which are designed to provide the science and technology we need to address the problem which already exists in the presence in the Great Lakes of the zebra mussels.
It is also very important, however, to understand that this government must continue with its actions of taking every step possible to ensure that ships coming into the Great Lakes from overseas waters are dumping their ballast at sea in order to ensure that no greater quantities of zebra mussels come into Canada than are already here.
We must continue to co-operate together in the future as we have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I asked what this government is doing that is effective. If the government was doing anything effective we would control the spread of the zebra mussel in Lake Huron and Lake Superior. We have to take immediate action today. We cannot wait two years to control the spread of the zebra mussel in the Great Lakes. If this government does something immediately we can control its spread in Lake Huron and Lake Superior.
What will this government do to correct the zebra mussel problem in these two lakes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important to understand that action for the sake of action is not always as productive as the hon. member suggests.
We are working in very close co-operation with the universities to ensure that we have the technology and science in place which will enable us to reduce the number of zebra mussels.
At the moment we are also considering using chlorine in water in those areas where intake pipes are being blocked by the zebra mussels. That is one action which is possible within a constrained area. However, it is also important to understand that you cannot put massive amounts of chlorine into water because that will create another problem.
The hon. member is suggesting that the work of scientists in Canadian universities is not important. I suggest to him that it is exceedingly important and the net result will be evident in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Last week the minister said that the independent truckers were satisfied with solutions proposed by him for the blockades
Oral Questions
and he said that the blockades would be lifted at international border points. However, several independent truckers in my riding and elsewhere say otherwise.
Can the minister now tell us precisely what he will do to assist the trucking industry and when he will do it?

Mr. Speaker, the the Minister of Transport for Ontario, Bill Wiye, and I, did reach an agreement with the independent truckers vis-a-vis what would be done by the province of Ontario and what would be done by the federal government to assist their situation.
Specifically, we suggested that we would crack down on illegal cabotage. We suggested that we would take up with the Bureau of Competition their complaints about certain U.S. truckers. Third, we undertook to try together to find a more effective way of collecting both the federal and excise tax on fuel and the Ontario fuel tax. We both agreed that a better method was necessary. We also agreed to have federal officials liaise with the committee with which they have.
The independent truckers were satisfied. The blockade has been lifted and the work is underway.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Why did the minister fail to notify the independent truckers of the so-called resolution to their concerns last week? Truckers at several crossing points, including Johnstown and the Thousand Island Bridge, were not notified.
Why were these independent truckers not notified at these border points?

Mr. Speaker, both the Ontario minister and myself put what we would do in writing and made every effort to communicate with the independent truckers. I think my hon. friend would understand that it is rather difficult to communicate without any organization being in place.
We made copies of my letter and that of Bill Wrye available to the Ontario Provincial Police. It is my understanding that through their network they were able to distribute it to the truckers.

May 30, 1990
Oral Questions

Concurrently the Conservative government members on the legislative committee examining Bill C-37 have refused to hear evidence from Quebec witnesses and limited public representations to only four groups.

Yesterday the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture learned of three serious cases of human rights violations at the Canadian RadioTelevision and Communications Commission. It also heard for the first time that the chairman of the commission had just heard of these violations.
The management of the CRTC is refusing to comply with the ruling of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. Will the Acting Prime Minister tell us why the CRTC is forcing its employees to extreme lengths in order to seek basic justice? If not, will he undertake to fully investigate why the CRTC is refusing to comply with human rights rulings?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
moved that Bill C-55, an act to amend the Customs Act, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to explain to the House very briefly Bill C-55, an act to amend the Customs Act. This bill proposes amendments to the Customs Act which will provide the Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, with the authority to implement fully recent amendments to the customs tariff.
If I may, by way of background, on January 1, 1988 Canada and most of its major trading partners converted their tariffs to the harmonized system of which I believe all hon. members are aware. The change over was certainly not intended to cause financial hardship to Canadian businesses. However, this could not be guaranteed because of the complexity of the conversion at that time. Therefore, the new tariff included Order in Council authority to allow the government during an
18-month period, after implementation, to respond to requests to restore the rates that existed before harmonization; in other words retroactively. Rate reductions are usually made retroactive to January 1, 1988, as outlined in the April 1989 budget.
The new customs tariff that implemented the harmonized system on January 1, 1988 included Order in Council authority to allow the government, during an 18-month period after implementation, to respond to requests to restore rates in effect under the old tariff, that is to say until June 30, 1989. A recent amendment to the customs tariff extends this authority for a further 12 months to June 30, 1990.
Currently the Customs Act does not allow for these provisions to be fully implemented, given that the authority to refund duties does not cover the entire retroactive period provided for in the tariff.
As a result, without an amendment to the Customs Act, importers will be unable to obtain refunds of duties overpaid and payments of accrued interest for the full retroactive period.
To remedy this I am proposing this legislation which does the following. First, it will allow the refund of duties where the Governor in Council has ordered that lower rates apply retroactively. Second, it will provide for the payment of interests on these refunds. Third, it will bring appeal rights into line with the new provisions.
In a nutshell, the purpose of this bill is to ensure that the Canadian business community continues to benefit fully from lower rates of duty established by the Governor in Council and that all importers are treated fairly and equitably.
I therefore count on the support of all hon. members of the House to pass this bill in a timely fashion.

Madam Speaker, as the minister has explained very briefly, this bill extends as I understand it to July 1992 the date by which changes can be made to the Canadian tariff schedule to assist manufacturers or importers who were inadvertently injured by the reclassification of tariffs which came about as Canada moved to the harmonized tariff system.
As the minister explained, this will allow the government to refund duties retroactively in cases where these increased duties were brought about simply as a result of this reclassification. Similarly, as the minister explained,
May 30, 1990

this bill allows payment of interest and appeal rights to importers or manufacturers.
This bill came about as a result of representations from business that it did not have enough time to assess the impact of changes arising from the reclassification of tariffs.
The bill is very straightforward. One cannot object to the help that is being provided to importers and manufacturers as a result of such a reclassification. On the contrary, I think we should support it. Our party is in favour of more liberalized trade internationally and this harmonized system of tariffs is indeed designed to ensure that there is more liberalized international trade.
While we can support the principle of this bill, it is appropriate to say that the government never hesitates to bring forward a bill to help businesses, but that it has failed to address the training and adjustment needs of Canadian workers adequately. It does not show the same haste and the same zeal when it comes to helping with the adjustment needs of workers.
I would like to remind this House and I would like to remind the minister that in 1988 the government established the advisory council on adjustment headed by Jean de Grandpre who at the time was the chairman of the board of Bell Canada Enterprises.
In a report tabled in March 1989 Mr. de Grandpre reminded Canadians of the abysmally low level of training done in Canada. In 1981, as incredible as it may seem, three out of four establishments in Canada did not provide any formal training to Canadian workers. These are figures that come from the de Grandpre report which was tabled in March 1989. In 1987, Canadian private sector expenditures on training were estimated at $1.5 billion, while American firms spent about $80 billion annually on staff training.
The de Grandpre commission had been set up in the context of the free trade agreement. In January 1988, at the time that this country was debating the question of free trade and liberalized trade, the government or the Prime Minister set up this commission in order to lead Canadians to believe that the government was actually serious about addressing the training needs of Canadian workers.
Government Orders
The major question that the council headed by Mr. de Grandpre had to address was: "Whether specific programs should be established to help Canadian companies and workers adjust to economic changes brought on by the free trade agreement".
The council decided that the answer to that question was no, that there should not be specific programs designed to address the effects of the free trade agreement because, the council argued, it is virtually impossible to attribute clearly and conclusively any particular economic event such as a plant closure solely to the effects of the free trade agreement. The same event might be attributed to global economic changes, to technological obsolescence, or simply to bad management.
Rather than recommending measures that were designed solely to help workers adjust to the effects of the free trade agreement, the council suggested policies to promote the swift reintegration into the workplace of workers displaced by changes of any kind. What they were talking about was the need for generalized policies. I do not think it is necessary today to go into any of the recommendations of the de Grandpre report in any great detail.
I would like to emphasize one such recommendation, which is that the government establish a corporate tax liability that would be offset completely if the firm provided a certain level of training to employees. It has now been over a year since the tabling of this report. It has been a year and a half since the free trade agreement came into effect and the government has failed to respond, to set up any generalized policies of this nature to correct the abysmally low level of training provided to Canadian workers by Canadian companies.

With respect to another issue, Madam Speaker, all members are familiar with the adjustment problems often experienced by older workers in our economy. A few years ago the government set up the Program for Older Worker Adjustment to help older workers who are victims of massive lay-offs. POWA provides support income to employees aged 55 or over who have been in the labour force for at least 30 years.
However not all workers are eligible under POWA, only those who are permanently unemployed as a result of a massive lay-off. Under the program such a major and permanent lay-off must have a serious impact for a

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
significant number of older workers. Exhaustive analyses are made to determine whether workers are eligible under the program. Among other criteria, in a community of 500,000 or more people, in a major Canadian city like Montreal where I live the minimum number of laid-off employees must be 100.
Madam Speaker, you can appreciate the injustices likely to arise from this kind of criterion. A few days ago I met with spokesmen for 13 laid-off Dominion Textile workers who were left jobless when the mill closed in 1988. About ten of these people are over 55 and, of course, the criterion concerning a minimum of 100 laid-off workers makes then uneligible for this program. I have a hard time trying to explain to these people why they are not eligible, because they tell me that aged 55, 57 or 58 as they are they have just as much difficulty landing jobs as a worker who was laid off along with 100 or 150 others. The number of lay-offs in a community has precious little to do with the ease with which a person might find another job, although that may indeed be a determining factor in a small community.
But in a big city of several million people, this may not be the most important factor. This arbitrary criterion in effect excludes many people who have as much difficulty as those who might be affected, as I was saying, by a lay-off of over a hundred employees.
Madam Speaker, I just heard my colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Leonard (Mr. Gagliano), who tabled a petition here, ask quite simply that this criterion be abolished. I think this is perfectly legitimate because in my opinion, the criterion should rather be more subjective, relate to the need felt by the worker instead of the number of employees who may be affected by the lay-off.

Those are just two areas that I wanted to point out in my remarks on the bill.
As I said earlier, the objective of the bill is laudable, and we support it. But we would like to see the government show as much concern in addressing the needs of workers who are affected by liberalized trade and other economic conditions as it does when addressing the needs of companies that are affected by liberalized trade.

Madam Speaker, contrary to the custom of this House to which I am trying to get accustomed, and unlike the previous speaker, I will attempt to speak to the bill. Having said that, I do not want to confine myself entirely to the rigidity of the tariffs.
The minister presents this bill as an innocent victim of a cabinet colleague. I hate to bring this out in public, but it is necessary to alert him to the fact that through this amendment he is sending a message to people that they will be able to filter through our borders with goods and escape paying their fair share of tariff.
Nothing is closer to the heart of the government than collecting every cent which it is due. Obviously, the purpose of this bill is to make amends for when the government has been over zealous and collected money it should not have collected. It will pay the money back, and it will pay some interest on it. That is laudable. I will not oppose that part of the bill, and I can tell the government it will not be defeated on the bill even if I do oppose it.
However, having said that, I want to bring to the attention of the House why this minister is being taken advantage of, unfortunately and without malice, by his cabinet colleagues.
On this quiet afternoon while the rest of Canada is fascinated with perestroika and glasnost, this little bill is called into the House not by design but by accident so that the Canadian people will not discover what is really happening with harmonization. The minister says he is very proud of the bill. When I am through, he will be shamed into altering some of it.
Now, I want to bring the minister's attention to something that is not allowing Canadian taxpayers to get their fair share of existing tariffs. That is not to say that we should work toward freer trade, but this government signed a free trade agreement, which was alluded to by the member who spoke previously. He also alluded to the de Grandpre report. May I say I agree completely with the previous speaker's assessment of the de Grandpre report. However, I will not make an analysis of that because I want to stick strictly to the tariffs.
As a consequence of the free trade agreement there are some businessmen who try to take advantage of loopholes. It is true, there are some business people out there who actually hire lawyers and accountants to seek out loopholes in legislation rather than pay their fair
May 30, 1990

share. At this point I do not intend to name names but as a matter of philosophy, there are some members of the capitalist community who think nothing of their social responsibility in ensuring that every penny due the government is paid, so they hire loophole lawyers.
Do you do your own tax forms, Dave?

I do my own tax forms, Mr. Minister. I do not go to those tax companies. I have so little income that it does not really matter.
Having said that, I will give advice to my colleague, should he seek it, on a separate matter. I am not soliciting business through you, Madam Speaker, but should that be the case my fees are quite fair, and under this tariff legislation I would be able to give him loopholes like he has never seen before-big enough to drive a truck through, a big truck. A train!
What kind of opening does this loophole provide? This is an opening for the Maquiladora program. Is the Maquiladora a household word that would be accepted in this august Chamber? It is indeed. It is not a swear word, but it is becoming a curse to Canadian workers.
Madam Speaker, I want to tell you that the Maquiladora program is a device initiated by some business people who are interested only in maximizing profits and taking advantage of a gullible government and an exceptionally kind minister who thinks no evil of anyone even though they are skinning him alive and, as a consequence, skinning the taxpayers.
This harmonization will legitimize the ugly little practice that is taking place now under the free trade agreement and the Maquiladora program, and sanctify a loophole that will mean the Canadian taxpayers get hosed again.
How does this happen?
I don't know. Tell us.

Well, I will tell you. I am glad you asked that question. I was not going to go into detail, but my colleague has asked me to do so. I know that some members of the House are breathless in anticipation of this big expose-today that will bring about front page headlines and perhaps cause the fall of this government.
Government Orders
If it wasn't for Gorbachev's visit the government would be finished after my speech today.
Tariffs became a subject of great interest to corporations as they saw the advantages from the elimination of other tariff structures between Canada and the United States after the free trade agreement was signed.
They also closed down businesses here in Canada, wrote off the closures as losses, and then went down to the Maquiladora zone and started a plant to do the same jobs they were doing here in Canada. What would be the advantage of that?
The same job that was paying $12 or $14 to a Canadian working person is now being performed in the Maquiladora zone between the United States and Mexico at $1.60 U.S. an hour. Now, consider the Canadian framework to protect jobs through an inherited system of previous Liberal and Conservative administrations, God rest their memories, good or bad. The tariff system was structured in a way that gave some limited protection to Canadian jobs and Canadian secondary and tertiary manufacturing. But, this government, in its haste to embrace the American flag, and the desire of a lot of those members of Parliament to run for the U.S. Senate, abandoned their option of determining some limited protection for Canadian workers.
My good friend from Montreal gave an excellent presentation concerning the de Grandpre report. I listened with interest. He made an interesting proposition that is available to us all. Since we are losing all the jobs, the government should at least keep its word to the de Grandpre commission to look after these people with social safety nets. What my good friend was talking about was an aberration of the agreement that is forcing workers out of jobs and on to welfare and unemployment insurance.
Tory planning.

A correct analysis by my colleague, Tory planning.
While the workers in Canada have been shifted out of jobs, and we have entered into a free trade agreement with the United States, we still have tariffs under GATT to protect some of the Canadian markets in other

May 30,1990
Government Orders
countries with whom we have not yet signed a free trade agreement.
Mexico, Maquiladora. The United States government came to a deal to set up this free trade zone. Mexican workers come across the border, work for $1.60 an hour and make components for secondary and tertiary manufacturing in the United States. And this is the shocker, and I want you to hang on, put on your seatbelt, Mr. Speaker. The clincher on this is that the Maquiladora program, which is taking jobs away from Canadian working men and women, manufacturing components for American products to be assembled in the United States of America are not, in every case, being stamped "Made in Mexico".
Why not?

My colleague says, why not? It is to take advantage of a loophole. By not stamping "Made in Mexico", because the products are made in the Maquiladora program, they can then be inserted into completed U.S. products and brought into Canada to avoid the proper tariff.
That is not fair.
That is not fair.
It is not honest.

It is not honest. As a matter of fact, it is true and it is not legal. Yes, it is true. Because it is true, the department was alerted to this concern. The bell rang. So, what did the government do? Did it hire a whole slew of new tariff collectors or customs inspectors at the border since the free trade agreement and the Maquiladora development?
Any prudent, thoughtful, cautious government that wanted to protect the taxpayers, would want to ensure that every penny coming to the government would come back. The Tories, who bleat nationally about their prudence, their fiscal responsibility-and they even have a cabinet minister who will not buy a new pair of shoes to bring down his budget as a symbol that they are concerned about every penny-how many new customs officers have they hired in the last year to watch the slip-over out of the Maquiladora unmarked components going into U.S. manufactured goods and coming into this country with lower and lower tariffs, after Carla Hills and our own minister signed a new agreement to accelerate the elimination of tariffs?
How many?
Well, I will tell you how many. Was it one?
No.
Was it 100?
One hundred?
No. Was it 50?
Maybe 50.
No.
What was it?
Was it 25? No. They have hired less than one dozen new customs officers since the signing of the free trade deal and-

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to interrupt my hon. friend but I know that he is inadvertently misleading the House. When he talks about this specific issue, he will know that we have put in place a number of verification teams who go out on a regular basis, south of the border, to verify specifically-
I am sorry to interrupt the minister but I do not think this is a point of order. It is more like a matter of debate. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca.

Thank you for your wisdom in pointing out that it was a matter of debate the minister wishes to enter into, not a point of order.
Since I am in order and I have assessed myself correctly-I have been in order ever since I came in here-I will continue with my comments. Yes, the minister in his interjection said they have assembled teams; I was coming to that and I am glad that he mentioned it. But that is not what I am talking about. What he has done is taken staff out of the existing staff complement-
I thought you were going to talk about the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening and talking and watching. I have been like a ferret, watching this government allow its-
May 30, 1990
A rattling rodent.

-watching its sense of responsibility slip away because they have been awed by Uncle Sam. These long, lost, semi-nephews, who think it is their manifest destiny to bow in front of Uncle Sam, have not taken on their responsibility through these tariff openings to collect every penny that is due us. I do not mind having the uncle, but he should not be painted as a tightwad like this government is doing, in refusing to collect the money from our uncle.
I am talking about this bill very clearly. As I described to you, Mr. Speaker, and with your rapt attention, I know you understand fully the description I am giving. The fact is that the Maquiladora program is producing secondary and tertiary products as components for finished American goods. They are not stamped "Made in Mexico" and, even though he sends out his flying squads to check, how can you check if the plastic component has no marking of origin and it is in the finished American product.
He can have 20 of his minions standing around looking inside the bowels of a toaster. I warn them not to put the plug in while they are sticking their fingers in the toaster. Some of them, like the minister, are not fully trained in their job and I want to warn them to pull the plug out first because there are other ways to get burned, like the free trade deal. Nonetheless, having said that, there is no way to identify the components. His squad stands around, shakes the toaster, looks at it and says, oh, there are no Mexican components here, it was all assembled in the United States. Of course they can say that because they have no method of checking back on what the Maquiladora program is creating in certain instances.
If you shake your head, I can hear it rattle.
My colleague, the minister, has a great sense of humour. He is the most trained minister that this government has.
You are skating around this.

I made no illusion to his figure skating background, he did it himself; but in this instance, you are on thin ice because you are allowing this open door into this tariff escapement. As a consequence, the Canadian taxpayers are being taken for a ride.
Government Orders
I recommend that the minister hire more customs officers and have them on the Maquiladora border. As a matter of fact, I would feel more comfortable if the minister would instruct his customs staff to go down to the Maquiladora corridor and catalogue what is being made there as components for finished American goods so that they at least know ahead of time what to look for. They have not made one single assessment over there of what is going on in the Maquiladora program and the impact it has on Canadian tariffs. Not one. They have not done that.
Negligence.

No, I do not think it is negligence. Negligence means a wilful decision not to do something. No, they do not even know what to do, which is even worse than negligence. No one over there has ever thought to send someone down to the Maquiladora program and get an assessment or a study to find out what is happening in the Maquiladora program and see first hand, on the Mexican side of the Maquiladora program, what components are being made and installed in American finished products and trans-shipped into Canada.
It is a good job you told them.
I am telling them now, and if they follow my advice-
Send you.
Send me? You come with me, we should go together. Mr. Speaker, I am not embarrassed, on occasion, to being seen in public with a Tory.
Especially a Tory like me.

If the minister wants to go along with me to Mexico, to look into the Maquiladora program, I will go with him and we will show the rest of his colleagues how they are being loopholed into losing millions of dollars by not collecting tariffs on this. We will go together. Let it not be said that the barriers between politicians are so great that they refuse to go to Mexico together in January for three or four weeks.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I want to state that whether or not the minister and I go to Mexico together, he should at least send some of his staff down and come back with a catalogue of what is going on. They never thought of this. Do you know why they did not think of this? They have been so busy playing politics and trying to survive, which is something that is foreign to most of the imperative that drives the members of this House,

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
because 99 per cent of the members in this House never think of politics, except on occasion. But when it consumes the government and it neglects to follow through on what is an open and obvious invitation for a loophole, the Canadian taxpayers lose again.
I do not blame this minister and I do not want anybody in the public to say that I am getting soft on this minister, but I think the real culprit is the Minister for International Trade, who is not available today. The free trade agreement is opening the huge loophole of the Maquiladora. We have records and analyses of the kind of subcontracting that is taking place in the Maquiladora program with cheap labour, and it is generally child labour, the unmarked components going into American goods and then trans-shipped into Canada without any tariff. Then we have this bill in front of us, with no assurance that the loophole is going to be closed.
I am not even debating the merits of free trade because that would be out of order. But, if I could debate the merits of free trade, I would point out, like other members of this House, what a very foolish agreement it was. I will not do that.
I am glad you did not do that.
I will not do that because I wish to maintain the dignity, the decorum, and the rules of this House.
Right on.
Laudable.

Thank you. Having said that, I did want to bring to your attention that it was the passage of that disastrous legislation that allowed this to take place. When we talk of harmonization, we are not talking about walking hand-in-hand. With this government, it may be walking but it is someone else's hand in their pocket and the consequences of someone else's hand in their pocket is that the Canadian taxpayer loses.
I would like the minister, when he responds, to stand up and say that he confesses he was not aware that this possibility existed through the Maquiladora program. I would like the minister to stand up and say that he will invite himself and myself to Mexico, and short of that, he will send a team down there to find out what is going on, and that he will table a report in this House to ensure all
Canadians that the loopholes that I have exposed will be closed.
I want to conclude by saying-
Conclude?
-because I have other speeches to make. I mean, what is the obvious reason why I should conclude now? I have a few more speeches, if you-
But the government should have learned by now.
What I am pointing out to you is, were this a Liberal administration, it would be just as bad.
No, no.
You're kidding!

Yes, yes, I do not want anybody to get the idea that I am just beating up on Tories for being dumb-bells. The other side of the coin is the Liberals who allowed this mess to happen in the first place because for years their whole tariff structure had been ignored and they did not beef up the customs department.
I am not saying that they would not do it if they were re-elected. I do know that they probably will keep the free trade agreement. I want to warn Canadians about that.
However, that would be a political statement. All I will do is repeat it. I want to warn Canadians that the Liberals will probably keep the same loopholes and keep the free trade agreement.
My party will not blithely be going along on this quiet afternoon with this little piece of legislation that does not appear to mean too much.
Madam Speaker, to your great satisfaction and joy, you will know that our party will oppose but cannot prevent this bill from passing. You will know that I have informed the Canadian taxpayers of this major loophole. You will know that myself and my colleagues will continue this struggle against the loss of money. You will also be happy to know that I intend to take my seat, satisfied that I have done my duty by making the government aware of this loophole, earnestly hoping that within a matter of hours it will withdraw this bill and correct the error of its ways.
May 30, 1990

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate with the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a few brief remarks on this bill because it would amend the Customs Act. There is presently a difficulty involving the Customs Act that has adverse effects on the constituency of Glengarry- Prescott-Russell. I want to assure the government Elouse leader that my remarks will be very brief.
This is an important issue that involves the potential loss of 165 jobs in the constituency that I represent.
I wish to tell the minister that I received a letter from a company in my riding known as McIntyre & Dodd Marketing Inc. It reads as follows:
I would like to draw your attention a loophole in our laws that an American company is making use of that if it continues may force us to close our Hawkesbury plant. Our plant in peak periods last year employed 165 people.
As you may be aware, the Canadian government a few years ago changed the dollar value amount on parcels that enter Canada from the United States through the postal system to be duty free if the value is $35.00 or less.
I understand that this does not apply in the case of parcels that are shipped across the border by parcel express, Purolator or other such companies. Only Canada Post has that particular exemption.
The letter continues:
The U.S. company in question, Direct Marketing Enterprises out of Westbury, New York, is using Canadian media to promote its mail order products with a return address in Windsor, Ontario. The orders are dispatched to a fulfilment operation in Detroit where the orders are processed and shipped to the border ready to be mailed at the closest Canada Post parcel centre. The average value of each parcel is under $35.00 therefore allowing the goods to be duty free.
I will not read the rest of the letter because I have made a commitment to the minister to raise this issue briefly.
However, I want to bring to his attention an ad that I have here in my hand from the French version of the TV Guide. It states, for instance, that a transistor radio is available for $14.95 and it describes it in the ad as follows:

"similar to those sold by other companies on television in the United States".
Government Orders
The implication is obvious, Madam Speaker. These companies advertise their products on U.S. television channels that are carried on cable, and then ship them to Canada duty free, making use of a loophole in the Customs Act that allows Canada Post to carry this merchandise from the other side of the border.
I know the minister is aware of this question, so I can be brief. However, I would like to ask the minister for a commitment to close this loophole, so that perhaps these jobs can be saved.

I am really looking forward to a positive response from the minister. Hopefully, we can save these jobs because there appears to be a loophole that enables these companies in the United States to utilize Canada Post- and I am not blaming the post office here although I do that on occasion in my capacity as postal critic for my party-in a clever way to ship parcels with a value under $35 across the border. They use this loophole in the law which is basically designed for families, I suppose, to send small gifts to relatives who live on the other side of the border.
These companies are benefiting this way and are causing a loss of jobs at Canadian mail order houses.
This company is located in Rexdale, Montreal and Hawkesbury. Its operations in my riding will be shutting down if this situation is not fixed rapidly. If it is not fixed it will create the loss of 165 meaningful jobs in my area where there is very high unemployment.
I thank the minister for staying a little longer than he intended. I am looking forward to his assistance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to answer briefly the concerns of my hon. friend.
As he pointed out in his comments, it is true that I am very much aware of this growing problem. I say "growing" because this law has been in place for many years. It is apparent that there are some organizations south of the border that are starting to abuse what was initially a good law to benefit families and other non-commercial uses, as the member pointed out.
I have already met on at least two occasions, and perhaps more, with individual business people who have outlined exactly the same concern, the latest of which was just a couple of weeks ago. At that time I told them, and I give my hon. friend the same commitment, that I would begin discussions immediately not only with my

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
officials but with officials from the Department of Finance to see how we could rectify the situation. I have brought it to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, with whom the final decision rests.
I do agree with my hon. friend, the people he represents and others in that same position that there is a semblance of unfairness here and we are going to take appropriate steps to correct it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to take a moment and thank the minister for his reply and indicate to him that I hope that among his colleagues and himself they can find a speedy solution. This is the type of thing which tends to move very quickly. The potential loss of jobs could occur very fast. I invite the minister either to review the legislation or the regulation, which may be necessary in this case, to change the rule in question and perhaps to ban the commercial usage of that provision.
I am not advocating that we create a situation which would make it difficult for families and so on to communicate with each other and to send a small parcel in the mail to each other.
If, for instance, the rule were changed in order to ban the importation of products using that clause for the purpose of resale, maybe that would accommodate what we are looking for and save these valuable jobs.
With that, Madam Speaker, I conclude my remarks. I thank the minister again for staying a little bit longer and providing this answer which I will take back immediately with me to my constituents with whom I am meeting tomorrow morning.

Madam Speaker, like other members I do not intend to delay this particular legislation because it is a useful response to change.
I want to take this opportunity to point out how discriminatory the government is being between one set of Canadians who are affected by changes in trade law and others who are also affected but who will be receiving no adjustment, no compensation or no response.
The changes brought about in the trade classification system are as a direct result of public policy. That was a decision made by government. It had nothing to do with external factors or anything else. It was part of our decision as a public sector to make changes that had some benefit to them.
The government in this case is accurately and properly recognizing that as a result of those classification changes certain businesses were faced with shortfalls. They were faced with changes in the tariff classification which created discrepancies in their income. I have no quarrel with that principle. It is fair.
If that is true for a business that is affected by a tariff change, then should it not also be true for workers who are affected by tariff changes? Is it not just as important for individuals who lose their jobs, who are dislocated or lose pension plans? Should they not have the right to some direct response?
We have raised the issue in this House, saying that commitments were made by the Prime Minister for a massive adjustment program. We have said that there were recommendations made by the MacDonald royal commission, which goes right back to the original source of the trade agreement, that major adjustment programs have to be made. Every time that issue has been raised we have been told: "We do not need it. It is impossible to tell. We do not know what adjustments are required because we do not know what is a trade related impact or trade related effect".
Yet the government finds it possible in this case to make that judgment and evaluation when a business or a company is being affected. However, when workers are being affected, that is not the case. In fact, what we have done is quite the opposite. We have substantially altered the unemployment insurance program.
I do not want to bring Bill C-21 up. It has been long and arduously debated in this House and in the other chamber. Nevertheless, the unemployment insurance system was the cornerstore of our ability to provide adjustments. Yet we have had a reduction of several hundred million dollars in that program. The principles in Sections 38 and 39 have been changed. Most important, Madam Speaker, as you well know since you have
May 30, 1990

heard the debates, there has been a withdrawal of direct participation of the government in the management of the UI program as a member of the commission. The government has turned it over to labour and business. Thus there is an abdication of public responsibility.
We are faced with an inherent contradiction wherein the government says: "We will use unemployment insurance to help compensate individuals affected by a public decision, and at the same time we pull out the membership of the public sector on the very commission that is supposed to provide the adjustments". The government is chasing its tail.
I simply want to refer the House to what I felt was an important report by the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre. This is a group that is chaired jointly by Shirley Carr and Thomas D'Aquino. Never have two stranger partners been part of the same issue. However, both business and labour are part of the centre for labour productivity because they recognize that the investment in human resources is key to what we do in the country.
In this report is a whole series of recommendations about what the government should be doing to improve the IAS, the Industrial Adjustment Services, to provide new programs for adjustment through unemployment insurance and to provide assistance, none of which has been provided.
I simply want to point out to members opposite that there is an unfairness here. I am struck by the celerity with which the government responded to the problem of the business community affected by tariff classification but has been so reluctant, so slow, so laggard in responding to the changes that affect workers. Surely, there has to be equity. Surely, there has to be fairness in the way the two are affected.
I would suggest to the Minister of National Revenue, who can provide tax write-offs and tax changes, to help workers adjust and change. There are communities being shut down. There are families being disrupted.
I just came from my office where I met with a group of people from the printing industry who have indicated that they have lost 25 per cent of their business to the United States since the inception of the FTA-one-quarter of their business. That is part of the major
Government Orders
rationalization. By rationalization they mean 500 workers have just lost their jobs at the Southam printing press in Toronto. That is being repeated across the country.
I do not know how many members have experienced in their own families the question of a lay-off or the loss of job, especially if it involves someone who is in their forties or fifties, an age when you have made your commitment to your profession for many, many years. All of a sudden that job can be pulled out from under you, not because you are a bad worker or because your company is inefficient. It is simply because of a change in Ottawa, a decision made by the government which it has a right to make, that all of sudden your livelihood is taken away.
For many workers-and I will go back to the old basic economic theory-the only investment workers have is their labour or what they have put into it over the years. All of a sudden it can be snatched away from them and the government in Ottawa will say: "We have no responsibility for that. We have no accountability. We have no special adjustment programs. We cannot determine whether it is trade related or not. I am sorry, you are simply going to have make do yourself". They are left on the scrap heap.
There are too many people on the scrap heap. We are facing a substantial build-up of those underutilized human beings in our society. I would think it should be a cause of some chagrin and embarrassment for our government to bring in a bill like this one which clearly recognizes its responsibility for one sector of the community and ignores the other sector of the community.
I simply wanted to use this occasion to make a plea on behalf of a large number of Canadians who are also affected by trade related changes, by reductions in tariffs, and by the new classification system. They are the people who work in those industries and who need some compensation or support because they have lost what is most precious to them. They are not the managers of big capital. The only real investment they have is the time, effort, and energy they have put into that job over the years. They deserve equal consideration, equal care and attention, and equal response and compensation by this government, something which it is providing for the businesses affected.

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
This is simply an argument based on the rightness of things. I ask the government to take into consideration that basic justice which needs to be met.

Madam Speaker, without wishing to hold up the debate on this bill, I would like to make a few comments on the speech by the hon. member for Winnipeg-South Centre (Mr. Axworthy) and ask him whether he has any statistics on the number of companies that might benefit as a result of this agreement with the United States, as compared with the number of jobs that will be lost on Montreal Island, for instance, a question I have been asking this government practically every other week.

Madam Speaker, unfortunately, there are no statistics on this particular question.
As you know, we suggested that the government set up a special commission to examine the problem of adjustment of Canadian industries to the impact of free trade. However, the government-the Minister for International Trade and others-said this was not necessary and that it saw no need for a study. Now we have a problem in this country. We do not know the extent of the impact of these changes on workers and industry. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue has statistics or figures for specific industries. In fact, the problem was predicted by the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre.
Unfortunately, we as members do not have the figures or sectoral studies for Canada. I think this is gross neglect on the part of the government because all the changes, all the layoffs we have been seeing for the past ten or twelve months since free trade are the result of legislation, and should therefore be dealt with by this government and Parliament.
