speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As you
know, Madam Speaker, the review of the Young Offenders Act has been a major priority of this government.
The government's objective in introducing this bill is to ensure that the Young Offenders Act, which was unanimously adopted by the members of this House in 1981, appropriately reflects the needs and values of all Canadians, including Canadian youth who come into conflict with the law.
The Young Offenders Act has come under criticism for its provisions for youth charged with violent offences, particularly murder. This criticism has come from the general public, judges, the provincial attorneys general, members of Parliament, and the media.
A few murder cases involving youths have attracted national attention and contributed to the public sentiment that the transfer mechanism and the sentencing in the Young Offenders Act should be revised.
More than this, these cases have called into question the integrity of the act as a whole and diminished public confidence in Canada's system of justice.
To respond properly to these concerns, a number of major steps has been taken in the past year. A comprehensive federal-provincial territorial study of youth charged with murdered was completed. It included a
May 30, 1990

case by case study in four provinces of all the youth charged with murder from 1984 to 1989.
A meeting of ministers responsible for juvenile justice was held on June 9 and June 10, 1989 at which the provincial attorneys general and the Minister of Justice for the Northwest Territories unanimously endorsed a resolution that the Young Offenders Act be amended in a number of ways.
An extensive consultation process was undertaken. A consultation document was released to over 100 organizations involved with young offender issues and to the provinces and territories. Bilateral meetings with key organizations were held.
All jurisdictions responded in the course of the consultations. About 80 non-governmental submissions were received and a national seminar took place in Ottawa. As well, we listened to the concerns of members of Parliament.
Bill C-58 addresses the three aspects of the act which lie at the heart of the concerns identified in our consultations. The first is the test to be applied by the court in determining whether to transfer a case to adult court. The second is the sentence available in youth court for youth convicted of murder. The third is the sentence and parole eligibility period for youth who have been transferred to adult court and convicted of murder.
I would like now to speak to each of these points. Numerous cases have gone before the courts as to how the existing transfer provisions would be interpreted. The proposed changes to the test seek greater clarity and equality in the interpretation of the law. The proposal would require the court to consider the objectives of affording protection to the public and serving the needs of the young person and to determine whether those objectives can be reconciled by the youth remaining in the youth system.
Where the court determines that these objectives cannot be so reconciled, Bill C-58 states that the protection of the public is paramount and the youth's case shall be transferred.
This test, while remaining consistent with the principles of the act, provides clear direction for the court and states that ultimately the protection of the public is paramount.
Government Orders
The transfer test would be applicable to transfer applications for all offences. We believe that the changes to the transfer mechanism will result in a more uniform interpretation of the law.
Bill C-58 also proposes that the maximum sentence for youth convicted of murder in youth court be increased to five years less a day. The sentence would be comprised of a custodial period which could not exceed three years unless an extension is subsequently ordered by the court.
The grounds for ordering such an extension would parallel those in the Parole Act, that is, where the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the young person is likely to commit an offence causing death or serious harm to another person.
Where no extension is ordered, a review hearing will be heard prior to the completion of the custodial portion of the sentence so the judge can set conditions which the youth will have to abide by in the community.
Where there is a violation of any condition the youth could be automatically returned to custody.
Finally, the bill proposes that the sentence of life imprisonment be retained for youth convicted of murder in adult court, but that such a youth be eligible for parole at an earlier period.
It is recommended that the parole ineligibility period be set by the sentencing judge somewhere in the range of five to ten years.
As you know, Madam Speaker, this only speaks to eligibility. The decision to grant parole is still made by the Parole Board.
This recommendation to reduce the period of custody that a transferred young offender must serve before being eligible for parole is strongly supported.
While the life sentence remains, it is believed that the reduction of the period of parole ineligibility will lessen the disparity in consequences which currently makes the transfer decision so stark for judges. In this way the justice system may be strengthened by allowing the courts greater flexibility.
Bill C-58 does not address the concerns of appropriate facilities and programs for violent offenders in either the youth system or the adult penitentiary system. This issue is very relevant at the transfer hearing stage as the judge

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
hearing the matter must determine which system is most appropriate in all the circumstances.
The resources in place in a given jurisdiction are a significant factor as individualized and well structured programs are viewed as a key to successful rehabilitation.
Beyond ensuring an appropriate response to youth charged with murder, many individuals and associations actively involved with youth have advocated a much broader based approach to violent youth. I whole-heartedly agree.
The first steps have been taken in the development of such an approach by inviting provinces and territories to join with the federal government in a collaborative study, the objective of which is to develop a systematic and financially viable approach to address violence by youth.
Hon. members may recall the Speech from the Throne in which there is a commitment to address not only the issue of violence but also the issue of treatment.
In fact, the issue of treatment along with issues pertaining to inadmissibility of evidence and custody have also been treated as priorities by the Department of Justice, the provinces and the territories. These issues were also the subject of consultations with the provinces, territories and non-governmental organizations involved with youth offender issues. There was not the same degree of consensus on what should be done. Therefore, more consultation with the provinces and territories is required.
In order to meet the federal commitment to respond to these issues, the Minister of Justice has proposed to her provincial and territorial counterparts that concrete proposals be put before ministers responsible for young offenders in June of this year in Niagara-on-the-Lake. I look forward to the tabling of the required legislative proposals in the fall of this year.
Bill C-58 will strengthen the justice system by allowing the courts to make the best decision in each case as to whether a youth should be dealt with in the youth or adult system. Also, Bill C-58 tries to balance the rights
of Canadians to security with society's long term interest in rehabilitating young people.
Protection of the public and rehabilitation of our youth are the key objectives of this bill. I ask the members of the House to support Bill C-58.

Madam Speaker, our party supports Bill C-58 and supports sending it to committee for study on possible amendments and new approaches that should be explored.
The basic theories of the bill are good. There is no question that public safety has to be paramount, as we have seen in other issues of criminal law administration. It has to be a major concern, but has not been so with this government. In the case of inmates in Corrections Canada's care, the paramountcy of public safety ranks about fourteenth. We are pleased to see, in this legislation, that there is a movement to have public safety paramount.
Also, it is laudable that the legislation is going to deal with the rehabilitation of young people. Quite frankly, our concern is that we are always dealing with half measures. As the former justice minister said: "This is a first step." We are continually taking first steps rather than taking all the steps that are necessary to deal with the problem. Dealing with young offenders is a major problem.
As originally introduced, the legislation was a progressive step in the proper direction. There is no question that it requires fine tuning. Why start with half solutions? Why not deal with all the problems? There is no question that the general changes dealing with criteria for applications to transfer to adult court from youth court are good.
There is no question that the change as far as the maximum period for incarceration for first and second degree murder is good; up from three years to five years. There is no question that early release and conditional supervision should be monitored more closely because of what we have seen in the past, particularly with the horrific situation in Scarborough.
There is no question that this legislation responds to the public outcry that has been generated by some cases. I know what effects public outcry can have. In my own area, I saw the effect of the escape of Allan Legere on the community.
May 30, 1990

This is a response to that. However, I think we have to go a step further and look at some other aspects. My colleague across talked about the unanimous resolution of the Ministers of Justice from the provinces. This bill has dealt with three or four of those recommendations, but it has left out a couple of important aspects. The Ministers of Justice or Attorneys General have asked that the act be amended to permit the admission of evidence of a voluntary statement. They have also asked for a greater flexibility to facilitate temporary release provisions to help rehabilitate young offenders. These are laudable objectives that have not been dealt with by the government.
Probably the more frightening aspect is this government's intention to get out of programs and to move away from financial commitments. The Attorneys General unanimously resolved that the recent unilateral decision to cap federal contributions toward provincial and territorial expenditures for young offenders represents a serious erosion of the federal government's commitment to the juvenile justice system in Canada.
It is interesting to note that there has been nothing done in this particular area to facilitate the operation of the system for young offenders. In fact, what we are seeing is a government intent on reducing its expenditures at the expense of young offenders.
It is time the government gets over this deficit-itis problem and moves toward dealing with juvenile crime, young offenders, and provides the necessary resources for the task.
There are other areas of concern with the legislation. As stated earlier, the Young Offenders Act amendments in Bill C-58 have not addressed the problems experienced by police in taking statements from young suspects and the evidentiary difficulties of introducing those in court.
Second, it has not dealt with the situation of the young offender being hospitalized for psychiatric treatment. The requirement of the legislation is that the young offender must consent. That obviously presents difficulties in the sense of trying to convince a person with those problems to consent to treatment. I do not think that is of any benefit at all.
We have to recognize in all this that habitual criminals, be they young offenders or otherwise, have to be dealt with firmly. Very serious crimes like first and second
Government Orders
degree murder have to be dealt with, and dealt with firmly. But, we must, however, be careful not to overbalance our response in that area to the detriment of the youth of this country and the young offenders who are caught within the system.
We must have a renewed commitment to help the youth of the country so that they do not become young offenders. Perhaps the best way to spend our dollars in this particular area is to make sure that the systems of housing and the ability to respond to youth are in place and properly financed so that we do not force young people to a life of crime.
We are supportive of this legislation going to committee. We are supportive of the basic thrust but we believe that first steps are not enough. We have to view the whole problem and take more than one step. We must take all the steps necessary to deal with this situation, to deal with the hardened youth criminal and the youths needing rehabilitation.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to stand this afternoon to address the very important issues which are covered by Bill C-58, the Young Offenders Act.
I must say that I am disappointed to hear that the Official Opposition has decided to support the principle of this legislation.
The effect of this legislation will be to ensure that more young people are transferred into the adult prison system and ultimately ensure that the level of crime in communities across this land will increase as a result of the demonstrated failure of society to deal with the prevention of crime among young people, instead of just dumping them into the adult criminal justice system.
I think it is important that we look back on the history of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the Young Offenders Act. I remember well the debate on the Young Offenders Act. I was here for that debate. I sat on the legislative committee that studied the legislation. We did a lot of work and we came up with a bill which, I think, moved the country forward. It was with a considerable sense of pride that we supported that legislation, as did all members of this House. That act was proclaimed in force on April 2, 1984. One of the most essential elements of that legislation, the Young Offenders Act, was a recognition that prison should be the last resort and that kids should only be sent to jail if there were no

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
other alternatives. The idea was that sending kids to jail ultimately is an admission of failure.
Indeed, one of the most important aspects of alternatives to imprisonment is ensuring that there are resources in place, so that when a judge must sentence a young person there is that range of alternatives which are set out in the bill. I said on May 17, 1982, some eight years ago, during debate on the previous legislation on the Young Offenders Act:
If this government is serious about improving and humanizing the system of criminal justice for young persons, it has to be prepared to put additional financial resources into the hands of provinces and territories to ensure that the legal framework which is established in the proposed young offenders act delivers a system which will indeed encourage young people to stay out of involvement with the criminal law. If indeed the federal government does not come up with additional resources, the provisions in the bill which provide, for example, for dispositions alternative to incarceration, will be redundant.
The provinces will argue that they cannot afford these provisions, and what we will see is an increased number of young persons dumped into jails for children. That is effectively what detention centres are. There should be disposition before an actual court appearance; in other words, diversion away from the criminal justice system. This will not take place unless the federal government is prepared to ensure additional resources are made available both to itself and to the provinces.
That was eight years ago. The bill took effect in 1984. What has been the history of our treatment of young people in conflict with the law since then? It has been a sorry history. It has been a history which has resulted in an increase in the level of crime among young people. It has been a history which has resulted in deep concern in communities across this land, whether it be in rural areas or in urban areas.
One of the most serious results of this is a dramatic increase in the level of imprisonment of young people. A study which was conducted by Raymond Corrado and Allan Markwart from British Columbia, both very learned professors who looked at the effect of the Young Offenders Act, said this: "It is clear that under the Young Offenders Act, B.C. youth courts have rather dramatically increased their reliance on incarceration as a dispositional sanction and correspondingly decreased their use of community sanctions, probation. This change cannot be attributed to a more general "get tough"
climate in the community that has affected the sentencing practices of the courts. There is evidence that not only are young offenders under the age of 17 years being dealt with more punitively than under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, but also that 17-year olds transferred to the jurisdiction of the youth court are now being incarcerated at a greater rate under the Young Offenders Act than they were in the adult criminal court."
That is the experience in the province of British Columbia. I am veiy pleased that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca is in the House today because one of the aspects of the New Democratic government from 1972 to 1975, under the leadership of that member, was a very enlightened approach to the question of young people in conflict with the law.
We recognized that we had to cut down dramatically on the use of jail as a sanction and indeed, former Judge Berger was appointed to head up a royal commission on the family and on children. He made some very progressive recommendations and I look forward to hearing from the member from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca because I believe that probably his very first involvement with the political process was in the area of juvenile delinquents back in the early sixties. We have a great deal to learn from the experience of that New Democratic government of 1972 to 1975.
Instead, the experience under this legislation has been deeply disturbing. I mentioned the study by professors Corrado and Markwart but we do not just have to look at academic studies. Let us listen to what our judges are telling us as well, about the impact of this legislation. In a decision last year Judge Ann Rounthwaite of Surrey, B.C., refused to sentence a 13-year old girl who had an insignificant court history to a lengthy jail term in order to keep her off the streets until a bed became available in B.C.'s over-crowded Maples Adolescent Treatment Centre.
In other words, there was such a desperate shortage of beds in the Maples that the Crown was trying to put this 13-year old girl in jail until a bed became available at the Maples. Put her in jail.
Judge Rounthwaite refused to do that. The judge said that the Crown counsel and youth court workers have repeatedly asked her to store problem children in an
May 30, 1990

open custody jail until they could be treated at the chronically busy Maples Centre.
These children are in desperate need of treatment and are often dangerous to themselves and others. They are not facing charges that would warrant the lengthy sentences necessary to keep them in custody until they could get into the Maples. Judge Rounthwaite went on to sentence the 13-year old girl to seven days in open custody and one year probation.
She talked of the despair that she felt, the fact that-and I am quoting from the judge now-a criminal court cannot use a sentencing process to make Holly Cottage, which is an open custody jail, an alternate to a residential treatment centre for adolescents with psychological or behavioural problems. Those branches of government responsible for providing such resources cannot shift their burden, difficult as it may be, to custody facilities or jail.
That is what we have been seeing happen across this country as provinces and the federal government refuse to accept their responsibilities to put in resources to assist young people before they get involved in criminal activity.
What has been the response of this federal government? Back in 1984 the Prime Minister answered a questionnaire from the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. He was asked about the priorities of a Conservative government in the area of young offenders and said: "The Progressive Conservative Party supported passage of the Young Offenders Act and continues to endorse its philosophy and principles. We are committed to assuring financial assistance to the provinces to allow for equal application of the law and availability of programs and services across Canada."
What has happened to that promise made by the Conservative Prime Minister of Canada? That promise has been broken. In May of last year the Conservative government unilaterally, without any discussion, imposed a cap on contributions to all of the provinces and territories under the juvenile justice services cost-sharing programs. Shameful.
Effectively, what this means is that for a five-year period the federal government is going to freeze its contributions at the 1989 level. That is a real cut every
Government Orders
year for the next five years. And who is it cutting? It is cutting young people in conflict with the law.
Ultimately the results of these cuts will be a greater level of crime in each and every community across this country. This from a government that talks about its commitment to law and order. By cutting back on funding for juvenile justice programs, this government is abdicating its responsibility for assuring that young people do not come in conflict with the law and ultimately abdicating its responsibility for safer communities, both rural and urban.
Obviously this decision is a breach of the promise that was made in the past.
Premier Tony Penikett, writing on behalf of all the ministers responsible for social services, wrote to the justice minister in March of this year. He wrote in his capacity as chairperson of the 1989 Interprovincial Territorial Conference of Social Service Ministers. He expressed his serious concerns about the effect of this federal cut-back in funding for young offenders. He said while it is accurate that the federal Department of Justice contributes approximately $160 million to programs under the Young Offenders Act, this does not even represent 50 per cent of the provincial-territorial expenditures under the act.
Premier Penikett notes that it is absolutely crucial the federal contribution grow by at least the cost of living each year in order to prevent the erosion of current service levels and to ensure equitable access across the country for young offenders, who require the cost-shared programs under the auspices of the Young Offenders Act.
What Premier Penikett is saying is that the Conservative government has betrayed the promises made in terms of adequate levels of funding for young offenders in this country. That is certainly unacceptable to us in the New Democratic Party. I am surprised and disappointed that members of the Official Opposition, the Liberal party, have not indicated that they, too, are opposed to the cuts in spending for young offenders. Their silence can only imply that they agree with the cuts that have been made. I hope that perhaps one lonely Liberal member of Parliament will stand in his or her place and speak out for our young people, speak out against the

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
federal cuts in programs to young offenders. I hope that one of them might stand and do that.
I see a member from Quebec. Let us look at the situation of young offenders in the province of Quebec. It is devastating. There are waiting lists of 22 months for boys who were sexually abused by up to 16 adults before they can get treatment.
Social workers in the Outaouais have pointed out that children who have been abused by their parents must wait while other cases take precedence because they do not have enough workers. In fact, the head of the agency has blamed the very serious delays on a logjam of cases and chronic underfunding.
The head of the agency has said that they have a choice between a 14-year-old and a baby. If we abandon the 14-year-olds, obviously, they will get involved in the kinds of criminal activities many of us are concerned about.
Earlier this spring, a report which was produced by Quebec's Youth Protection Committee condemned the Outaouais service for the lengthy delays and waiting lists that young people face before cases are dealt with. In fact, the president of the Youth Protection Committee in Montreal stated that Quebec society should feel a collective shame that the situation has been allowed to drag on as long as it has. Some 3,000 children in the province of Quebec are on similar waiting lists.
As Mr. Dowie stated, children need protection. You do not keep them on a waiting list for 22 months. You do not keep them on a list for five months. You deal with them now. That is why we have to talk about prevention instead of the kind of narrow approach of simply throwing more kids in jail for longer terms. We also have to recognize the other elements of prevention.
We have to recognize that far too many youths in trouble with the law have learning disabilities. It has been estimated that something like 70 or 80 per cent of young people involved in crimes and criminal activities have learning disabilities. What are we doing as a government to deal with that concern? Nothing, absolutely nothing.
What are we doing to deal with the problem of violence on prime time television and weekend children's television. Look at the cartoons. It has been
estimated that the average child, during his or her childhood, sees something like 10,000 murders on television. What kind of impact does that violence on television have on the psyche of our young people?
The kind of aggressiveness, the Rambo mentality, which is all too common on television clearly must be reflected in the behaviour of our children. As a society we are failing our children by allowing that violence to continue.
The response of the government in this legislation is to make it easier to transfer young people to the adult courts and ultimately into the adult prison system. That is not the answer. We all recognize the concerns that people feel about violent acts committed by young people, particularly murder.
We all recognized the sense of outrage that the community felt at the Scarborough case when a young murderer was sentenced to a term of three years. After that, he was out on the streets. Obviously, communities do not accept that.
There is provision for transfer in the existing Young Offenders Act, and these provisions have been adjudicated by the Supreme Court of Canada. Indeed, the provisions for transfer can and should be used in appropriate circumstances. Because of some incidents that have given rise to understandable concern on the part of the community, it does not suggest that we have to change the test for transferring all young offenders. Surely, it is a step backward.
What it will do is dump more young people into adult prisons, not just after they have been convicted, but while they are waiting for trial. One serious concern raised by the Canadian Council on Children and Youth is the failure of this legislation to deal with the problem of young people who have been transferred to adult court who are awaiting trial and, while awaiting trial, are locked up in adult prisons. They can be locked up for months.
What does the government have to say about that? Nothing at all. What does the government have to say about young people who are 15, 16 or 17 years old, after being convicted, following transfer and serving their time in adult jails? Absolutely nothing. Apparently, it is acceptable to the government. It is not acceptable to New Democrats, and we intend to speak out on this in committee and when the bill comes back to the House. A
May 30, 1990

number of my colleagues will be taking the opportunity to speak from a variety of perspectives.
The hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt, a rural community, will be speaking on the legislation from the perspective of a rural member. He pointed out when speaking very eloquently to other members of caucus that, in fact, in rural communities young people do grow up earlier. In many cases, they are out driving, working and playing a responsible role in the community at the age of 14 or 15. He urged all of us to recognize that we cannot necessarily apply the same standard to urban and rural communities. He is right.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca pointed this out as well. We must respond to young people as individuals and deal with their tragedies individually. We should not follow the mindless trend of throwing them in jail for longer periods of time, or throwing them into adult jails.
Even the Chief of Police in Edmonton said in an interview just last year: "Increasing murder sentences for young offenders would be useless in dealing with youth crime." Chief Bob Claney of the Edmonton police force said: "The proposed changes are only a distraction and will not make a significant impact on the problem of teen crime." Chief Claney is on the front lines and is telling us: "Look, this is not the answer."
Instead, what does he say? He says that he would rather see the provincial and federal governments provide more counselling for the vast majority of young offenders rather than stiffer penalties for the tiny proportion who murder. I quote from Chief Claney. He says: "If we are successful with a youngster, he will not end up in adult court." He is right.
We cannot overestimate the impact of murder on our communities, whether it be a young person or anyone else. We also have to put it in context and recognize that murder is something like one-fortieth of 1 per cent of all the offences that are dealt with in youth court. In our understandable desire to respond in a serious and appropriate way to murder, we must not condemn hundreds of other young people to being dumped into the adult prison system and ultimately condemn them to a further life of crime. That is an abdication of our responsibility as a society.
Government Orders
What about a group of young people who are at risk more than any other? I speak now of aboriginal youth, native youth. We received a very powerful submission from the National Association of Friendship Centres. They asked us to recognize that this bill is not the answer to juvenile crime either among aboriginal youth or other youth. They give us some appalling figures around the area of aboriginal youth and crime. They point out that aboriginal youth are more likely to be charged by police for offences than are non-aboriginal youth, that aboriginal youth are more likely to plead guilty than non-aboriginal youth, that aboriginal youth are more likely to receive longer and harsher penalties, that aboriginal youth are more likely to be transferred to the criminal court system-and this bill will make that even easier- and that aboriginal youth are more likely to receive "secure custody orders", that being another term for jail.
Let us look at the figures for young aboriginal people in jail. The Manitoba Metis Federation reported that in Manitoba 92.8 per cent of the young women held on remand were native and 47 per cent of the young men held on remand were native. That situation is a national scandal. It has been described as a national shame by the chief commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission and this government is cutting back on funding for juvenile justice programs.
Let us look at some figures on secure custody and open custody. The open custody unit of the Manitoba Youth Centre held 87.5 per cent native girls and 55.5 per cent native boys. In the secure custody unit of that jail, 100 per cent of the young women were native. So this government comes forward with legislation that makes it easier to dump young native women and men into adult jails. That is not the answer. That is surely not the answer to the devastating problems that face our youth in this countiy, whether they be aboriginal youth or other youth.
There are answers. The Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science some years ago produced an excellent report entitled "Child at Risk". It pointed out that society can identify at a very early age those kinds of conditions which will lead to a life of crime. Yet we are cutting back on funding to respond to those concerns.

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
Child abuse has been recognized as a very significant factor in the development of violent criminal behaviour in later years, but in the past our society has paid more attention to cruelty to animals than we have to cruelty to children.
We have to deal with the question of child abuse. I have talked about violence on television. I have talked about the question of poverty. One of the most direct links that can be established between crime and young people is the linkage of poverty. In fact, the National Council on Welfare published a report in 1975 called "Poor Kids". On what it means to be poor in Canada the report says that to be born poor is to face a greater likelihood of ill health in infancy, in childhood and throughout your adult life. To be born poor is to face a lesser likelihood that you will finish high school, lesser still that you will attend university.
On that I might add that a young native person in Canada today has a better chance of going to jail than of going to university.
Or committing suicide.

Or of committing suicide, as my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca says.
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood that you will be judged delinquent in adolescence and, if so, a greater likelihood that you will be sent to a correctional institution. To be born poor is to have the deck stacked against you at birth and to find life an uphill struggle ever after. To be born poor is unfair to kids.
Well, Madam Speaker, they were right in 1975 and they are right today. Fifteen years later we still have over
500,000	kids in this country dependent on food banks in order to survive. We still have kids, not just in inner cities but in rural communities as well, going to school hungry. What is this government doing to respond to these concerns around child poverty? It is doing nothing, nothing whatsoever. What is it doing to deal with the problems of foetal alcohol syndrome? We know the impact that that can have as well on a later life of crime. The government is doing absolutely nothing.
We are presented with a bill by a government which says that this is its answer to the concerns around the question of young people and crime.
This is not the answer of the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. The Canadian Council on Children
and Youth is a broadly based body which held extensive consultations around this legislation. It has come to the conclusion that the legislation is a step backward and not a step forward.
There are some elements of the legislation that we do support, there is no question about that. Under the legislation a young person who is transferred to adult court and faces a sentence of life imprisonment for murder will be eligible for parole anywhere between five and ten years after they start to serve their sentence. Under the existing provisions of the Young Offenders Act, a judge is faced with a very difficult choice; either treating such young offenders as young offenders in youth court with a maximum term of three years or transferring them to adult court, in which case there is a maximum of life imprisonment with no eligibility for parole for 25 years.
That was the trade-off in 1976 for the abolition of capital punishment. As a society we have to ask ourselves, not just in the case of young people but in the case of all prisoners, whether the price we paid was not too high and whether we should not be re-examining the issue of the date for parole eligibility because our prisons are filling up rapidly with people who have been convicted of first degree murder and are not eligible for parole for 25 years. Surely that is a concept that we should, in fact, re-examine.
I have touched on some of the issues that we as a party want to address, I have touched on this government's failure to adequately fund services to young people and on the question of prevention.
Another concern is that of prevention in terms of programs for young people who are involved in drug and alcohol abuse. You would think that governments, both provincially and federally, would be doing everything in their power to ensure that these programs were adequately funded. Yet we hear over and over again that there simply is not enough space for young people who are abusing substances, whether it be alcohol or drugs.
We are abdicating our responsibility to young people who have been sexually abused and physically abused. We are abdicating our responsibility to poor kids. We are abdicating our responsibility to kids who are involved in alcohol and drug abuse. Instead we are making it easier to transfer them into the adult prison system. Great answer.
May 30, 1990

We in this party believe that the emphasis must be, surely, as the Canadian Council on Children and Youth has focused, on rehabilitation of those young people who have come in conflict with the law but, most importantly, on doing everything we can as a society to prevent young people from coming into conflict with the law in the first place. To the extent that they do, they should be dealt with with compassion and with understanding, but also with firmness, because that is what our society asks for as well.
I could go on at some length about the absence of psychiatric services. I have spoken about the question of learning disabilities and the chronic shortage of psychological services.
Adequate child care.

Adequate child care, as my colleague from Saanich-Gulf Islands has pointed out, is another area which is of great importance. We are still waiting for the government to keep its promise for a national child care program. That as well would go a long way to assisting in reducing the level of crime among young people in this country.
I want to conclude by expressing some disappointment, first in the response of this government to what is clearly a crisis involving young people and crime in this country. It could have come up with a thoughtful approach that would emphasize prevention and rehabilitation which would not involve cutting funds to provinces and territories as it has done. Instead, it has put together this piecemeal approach, an approach which, unfortunately, is guaranteed to fail.
I am also disappointed that the Official Opposition, the Liberal party, is supporting this approach. Liberal members have stood in their place and said that they agree with and support these principles.
Where are the members of the Liberal party when it comes to cuts in funds for juvenile justice? Why are they not speaking out for more funding for juvenile justice programs, instead of supporting the Conservative government in its cuts?
These are some of the issues that I wanted to address in the few minutes that I have had an opportunity to speak on this legislation.
Government Orders
I want to close by reminding the House of the words of a very distinguished judge, Judge David Bazelon, who just recently retired from the United States Circuit Court of Appeal for the D.C. Circuit. He said this: "Children who come through the courts are living evidence of the failures of our society to provide the basic necessities of a healthy, mental and physical life for all too many of those we call society's most precious resource. If we refuse to invest in our children, we can only expect more of the same".
Let us listen to that message. Let us invest in our children. Let us not take a step backward with regressive legislation that will result in more children in adult jails and more crime in communities across this land.

Madam Speaker, first, I want to compliment my colleague for making a very reasonable and emotional appeal combined in a very forthright manner.
I regret that this is not of paramount importance to every single member, but I know that every member considers it an issue that affects themselves and their communities.
One of the reasons in my opinion that this remains a problem in terms of having adequate services for children in our country is the simple fact that children do not vote. Another compounding factor is that rich children do not go to jail. Middle class children rarely do, but poor children go to jail frequently.
When I first entered politics 30 years ago, I had come to politics out of jail. I am the only politician who left jail and came into politics, instead of the other way around. But I want to confess that I worked there. I was not sent there.
I spent my life, up until I came into politics, committed to working in the corrections system. At a very early age, I was so employed and discovered that what I had been taught in university and what I had assumed was taking place in institutions was indeed what was really taking place. I discovered other things that shocked and motivated me to come into politics.
Since I only have a brief few moments, I want to share with this House what goes on with a child after an offence has been committed and understanding that there is no structure whatsoever mandating care, protection or counselling for the victim. Let us get that on the

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
record. The focus is on punishment with absolutely no care for another child victim of a crime.
For those who suggest that an alternate plan to what the government is suggesting is bleeding heart, let me tell them that victims of crimes in this country, especially children, are the most abandoned group in our society. If this government were concerned about children, the first thing it would do is include in the act a guarantee that any child who is sexually abused, any child who is victimized physically or psychologically by anyone, young or old, is given by law a guarantee of the best possible services available to that child. Only then would I believe the motivation was totally in protection of the community-
It is on the record and we understand that the victims are only part of an ongoing system and have no care of real value in this whole process.
Let us take a look at the 16-year old boy who comes into court and who has been convicted of a violent crime after being transferred to an adult court. If that young boy has been in a remand centre for three or four months awaiting trial, then that child has already been the victim of gang rape.
This is not a very pleasant subject, but we should deal honesty with what takes place in our institutions. Any young boy who comes into an adult institution, either on the remand side of the institution or in the main population of the jail, or is exposed to the access of the main population of jail, is the victim of gang rape within a matter of weeks. Lots are drawn. This is the nature of the institution. These are not happy subjects, but this is the reality that members of this House should know so that they understand what they are doing when we pass this kind of legislation.
That young boy is guaranteed to be physically assaulted in that institution. That assault leaves indelible scars in the mind of that youngster forever. No matter what the system then attempts to do, let me tell you, Madam Speaker, that the indelible experience that that child had in the institution scars that person for life.
Recently we read about a 27-year-old who is a threat to society because that young man is a paedophile and there is no protection in our structures to ensure that the community is protected from such an offender. Once being a victim of that kind of crime, the victim turns into the offender more often than not. The state guarantees, because of the institutionalized structure and the experience, a supply of offenders. Having been victims leads to the offence.
I want to leave that aside because I only have about eight or nine more minutes. I want to talk about young women in our society and something that happens to young women who come into court that is not really understood by a large body of legislators.
Young offenders still can be charged with incorrigibility. Incorrigibility can cover range of behaviours that are unmanageable by society-a range of behaviours that does not lead to cheating on the stock market, a range of behaviours that does not lead to cheating on income tax, a range of behaviours that are snickered at by adults, but a range of behaviours by youngsters that are totally out of control that could not be applied as a measure of judgment to adults. Young girls, young women, are charged with incorrigibility by way of promiscuity. I have yet to hear of a young male who is charged with incorrigibility by way of promiscuity. It is a double standard in our society.
I want you to understand that quickly and clearly a male dominated society says to a young 13-year old or 14-year old girl that she may not be promiscuous, but that is not an attitude which is held in the case of a young boy.
That young girl, who is charged with incorrigibility by way of promiscuity, is institutionalized. She was institutionalized in my own province of British Columbia at one point in an institution called the Willingdon School for Girls-a young woman who is expressing severe emotional trauma in her own home situation or foster home situation, who knows of no way of dealing with it other than being a victim of crime, who has probably been sexually abused as a young child at the early age of four, five, or six in patterned behaviour that is indelibly imprinted on that child's mind and who assumes that is a normal pattern of behaviour that she must live through for the rest of her life.
Once placed in the institution she is not given access to the separate, individual, loving care that is necessary for any such child. Once placed in an institution she is grouped with other young women who have similar or more severe problems, and what appears to be an
May 30, 1990

abstract problem for this young woman becomes the norm in the group that she is in.
No consistent treatment pattern takes place. As a matter of fact the kind of learning pattern that takes place in such institutions, duplicated not only in Canada but right across North America, guarantees a supply of chronic offenders who have been scarred in youth in these institutions.
I said in an earlier speech that at one time 60 per cent of the female population of the Kingston Federal Penitentiary were graduates of the Willingdon School for Girls in British Columbia. When the institution was closed there was a dramatic drop in repeated patterns of behaviour because the pattern of behaviour was not reinforced in an institutionalized setting for which the community was paying.
What were the options? We sought and purchased, case by case, the kind of treatment plan that was essential for each one of these young women. That is no longer available. As a matter of fact in the 30 years I have been involved in public life, with a concern, essentially my own private driven concern about why I am in politics, we have actually gone back. We have actually made the situation worse, not better.
Little did I think that I would be in a situation in 1990 dealing with a bill that again is a cosmetic to dampen political fears. It is a knee-jerk reaction to public outcries against violent crimes.
It is not a first step, as my colleague who is a Liberal member said. It is a continuous misstep of legislation that is often implemented on a knee-jerk basis without any sense of history, any sense of proportion, or any sense of what is happening to these young people. They are not rich. They are not middle class. They are poor children, essentially neglected and dropped into the institutions of our society, whether it be foster homes or the other kinds of institutions we have.
What we experience here in this country is minuscule compared to our neighbour to the south. But we have not learned, nor have they.
I know my time is almost up, but I want to say that we are culpable as politicians. We are the ones who are in effect the wrong ones. We are the ones who are making the mistake. We have an opportunity and a responsibility
Government Orders
to protect our total society. The only way to protect our total society is to ensure that our children are protected-the criminal element and the victim. We turn the criminal element into a guaranteed supplier of violence. We turn the victim into a repeat pattern of that behaviour. None of this legislation deals with that.
Simply said, it does not take a genius to figure out when a child is in trouble. Any neighbourhood has parents who sit down at a table and say: "If somebody does not do something for Suzy or Johnny soon, they will be in trouble". Those parents are right. They are in trouble. This bill does nothing to stop that. This bill does nothing for treatment, nothing to protect the community, nothing for services to the victim. It guarantees a constant supply of adult criminals coming through this kind of system.

Madam Speaker, I think the House has been treated this afternoon to two very good speeches, one by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway and the other by my esteemed colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. Both of them have a fundamental understanding of the problem.
I know that our society, especially now, seems to be reaching out increasingly for simple solutions to very complex problems. I guess that is a human way to deal with a problem. You want the quick answer. There is no quick answer.
This bill is an attempt at a quick answer. What young offenders need is love and understanding. As a mother of two teenagers, it offends me that this is the government's response to the woes of young people in Canada.
I want to ask the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, with his vast experience in corrections and his esteemed reputation in the political field, if he would expand on the links between poverty and crime among young offenders.

Madam Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I appreciate the hon. member's comments. I want to suggest to this House that nobody has a monopoly on what the answers are. I can repeat that the consistent answers have been wrong most of the time.
There is a distinct link between young people who end up in courts and the fact that they have very little financial backing. A wealthy person is not able to prevent a child from having aberrant behaviour but is able to mobilize the best possible services to protect their child

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
when that child is confronted with the legal consequences of his or her actions.
In other words, if an upper middle class or an upper class child has committed an offence that warrants prosecution under legislation such as this, that child goes into court with the best possible back-up services of lawyers, psychologists and those people in the medical profession, the psychiatrists who claim to have some answers about child behaviour.
That array of service is not available to a poor child. That array of service is not even available, I regret to say, to a child who is a ward of the state, albeit in some provinces there is an effort to maintain a modicum of protection for that child who has been through perhaps 16, 17, or 18 different foster homes by the age of 12, 13, or 14.
That is the past of the individual child who is the ward of the state and appears in court. It is not unusual to have some children having been in 12, 13, or 14 different foster homes, not knowing one consistent set of parents. Let us extrapolate the situation to what my colleague said about the indigenous people. Let us look exactly at what we have attempted to do to those children who come into trouble with the law and our method of dealing with it.
We ignore the indigenous people's own inherited culture. We immediately take those children out of the only social experience they have. It may be one that we as Europeans make an abstract judgment about. Because it is a different culture and because it does not match our culture, we snatch the child. That was the exact word I heard as a young social worker. We "snatched" children from indigenous people. They are poor. Is my time up, Madam Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This being the period for questions and comments, I saw that other members seemed to be looking forward to asking questions.

Madam Speaker, it will be my fault that I lose my whole 10 minutes, but I will go on with my train of thought.
An indigenous child is immediately extracted from the only culture that it knows, dumped into ours, brought into the courtroom, and dealt with either as a foster child or a ward of the state. If you expect that child to have a
chance as my colleague asks on the basis of fairness, forget it.
It is not a story that I have made up. The statistics given by my colleague are absolute proof of what is going on for young women and indigenous children. They do not have a chance if they are poor and they appear in juvenile court in this country.
Granted, there are judges in juvenile courts who cry out for better services, who sit in judgment of these children and go on record day after day proclaiming their horror and shock at the absence of services for children. Those proclamations fall on deaf ears of legislators who have heard the tale of woe and respond only by this foolish legislation that is being presented now.
It is not the fault of the courts. Most people who work in the system understand exactly what is wrong and have said so in testimony to agencies and to committee, all to be ignored, and ignored again in this legislation.
What can I say? A rational, thoughtful, prudent government would gently pull the bill back and say that there is no excuse now to say that there will be parallel accords to this bill. There is no excuse now to say that at some future date we will deal with these problems. There is no excuse to suggest that this is a placebo. The reality is that we should have the whole package now. If we save one child it is worth the whole package, but we are not doing it and that is why we are opposed to this bill.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my colleague for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca for the usual passion which he brings to this House and his personal experiences which make the debate much more meaningful to everyone who sits in the House. I notice that a lot of people stop and listen for that reason, myself included. I have a great deal of experience as well with native children in the educational system and even though I participated on a daily basis with that kind of circumstance, I am still appalled and somewhat amazed that those kinds of statistics are staggering even to one who was involved in the situation.
My friend used the term "knee-jerk" reaction. My concern is that when the whole system is broken, I do not think you can tinker with it. I suggest that perhaps two years from now there will be a further tinkering to this system when, in fact, the entire system has to be
May 30, 1990

reworked. It is like repairing an old vehicle, eventually there is a time when you must scrap the vehicle and start with a new one.
My question to my friend is, should all of the legislation be reviewed and rather than tinkering with the system, just change the whole process?

I do not have all the answers. I do know that the current vehicle is the wrong vehicle and it is very expensive. If one wanted to make the case purely on money, throw out the current system. The money we spend to house a child in an institution ranges between $40,000 to $60,000 a year. We should spend that kind of money on preventive services for the children who are destined for trouble. A quick change would be to integrate preventive services into a day care program, into kindergartens and into grade schools.
Just as the health community is talking about AIDS education for children who are pre-teens, we can surely move into behaviour problems in pre-teens within the education system. The scourge of AIDS is forcing us to rethink our whole approach to education. I am not suggesting we see a similar scourge, but surely the consequences of neglecting our children and leading to the kind of patchwork of services that guarantee an adult population in our prisons should have the same dramatic scrutiny as the problem of AIDS.
I have some answers and suggestions. Mine may not be correct, but surely to goodness the one common thread that runs through all of our experience in this field is that the earlier you get to the child and his or her parent or parents and deal with the problems quickly, the less chance there is of that child growing up to be the menace to the community that he or she may be.
One last comment in that regard. When my colleague suggests, as the bill has, a provision to release people after five years or 10 years, it sounds humanitarian, but in many instances we wait until the end of the parole period before we release someone because their behaviour in the institution does not warrant it. I just want to address the logic of that for a moment.
Government Orders
The well behaved offender who is released early is not the person we are concerned about; it is the ill behaved offender who is not released because his or her behaviour in the institution is not conforming who we should worry about. If we are concerned about society, it is that offender who needs a supervised period in the community. To wait for sentence to be finished because the parole board says we cannot take the risk means that we are dumping high-risk people into the community and with no services whatsoever.
There is a whole range of recommendations, I would like to suggest to my colleague. All of this has been heard by parliamentary committees since 1936. It is all on the record of this Chamber and of parliamentary committees since 1936.1 think the first one was the Archam-bault commission. It is all on record, all there, all documented, and all universally ignored.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The period for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate, the hon. member for Victoria.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to this bill as the assistant justice critic for the New Democratic Party and a member of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General. I will oppose the bill on second reading, as will the New Democrats in Parliament.
It is interesting and discouraging to me that it is clear that the Liberals will be supporting this bill. It is a bill which completely fails to deal with both the public concern and the reality of problems with young offenders, created in part by the Young Offenders Act. It completely fails to deal with the difficulties in this area.
It is of some interest and concern to me as well, if I can say in a preliminary way without breaching the rules of this House, to see the lack of interest in this bill on the government side and on the Liberal side in this House. I note that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice is in the House, but the tradition in this House has been for cabinet ministers themselves to attend, particularly the important second reading stage, a tradition which-I have not yet suggested there is an absence in the House-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On a point of order, Madam Speaker.

May 30, 1990
Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think that a point of order by the hon. parliamentary secretary will be necessary.
The hon. member for Victoria started by stating that he knew what should normally be done in this House and then proceeded to do exactly the opposite. I think it would be better for the hon. member to continue with debate. The hon. member for Victoria.

I appreciate the implied admonition Madam Speaker, and perhaps I can simply say that the tradition of having ministers here is a valuable tradition and is one which I know this House fully respects.
The public is concerned about young offenders and that concern in part has been generated by a few examples of horrible crimes committed by young offenders and for which the public sees insufficient sentences handed down. Those few cases have led to a strong feeling amongst the public that the law is "too lenient". This attitude has been reinforced by such organizations as the Canadian Police Association, which has expressed itself in forceful terms.
I have the communication from the Canadian Police Association dated October 3, 1989, which reports on the resolutions adopted at the Canadian Police Association convention in 1989. One of the resolutions specifically dealt with young offenders. Again, the Canadian Police Association was speaking to an entirely legitimate concern; it is the conclusion that has been misunderstood by the government. The resolution reads as follows:
WHEREAS the Canadian Police Association, representing 32,000 police officers across Canada, believes that the Canadian people are not well served by some of the current provisions of the Young Offenders Act, particularly in the areas of transfer and sentencing of young offenders charged with murder, and other serious offences,
AND WHEREAS a consultation paper dealing with possible amendments to the Young Offenders Act has been circulated by the Department of Justice,
BE IT RESOLVED that the Canadian Police Association make representation to the Government of Canada to have the Young Offenders Act amended to better protect the people of Canada from violent young offenders.
The Canadian Police Association goes on to complain in another resolution about what it sees as the watering down of the mandatory 25-year sentence for murder. It,
in fact, reaffirms its support for what it is pleased to call "the supreme penalty", i.e. the death penalty.
The fundamental error that the Canadian Police Association makes is to make the assumption that the law itself is the cause of the problems and, second, that amendments to the law can "better protect people from violent young offenders". It is disappointing to me that the police officers of Canada, as represented at least by their association, have not offered to the government the kind of lessons and experience that I know that police officers of the grass roots understand, which is that the causes of crime and particularly the cause of young offenders crime is far more complicated than is represented by the mere suggestion that amendments to the Young Offenders Act is going to help one way or the other.
The causes of crime by young people is at one level complex and difficult and is individual to each case; and at another level is a symptom of the illness in our society and our failure as a Parliament to require the government to show comprehensive leadership in the whole area of justice and social equity in our country.
Individuals who commit crimes, whatever age, have some responsibility for those acts. It is important as the parliamentary committee now known as the Daubney committee from the last Parliament noted, that offenders begin to understand the responsibility they have for their acts and take responsibility not only for their acts but for their lives.
Even more important is that the government and society generally must understand the responsibility that we have for the conditions which create crime. This is at both a macro and micro level. First, at the macro level, it is absolutely clear from study after study, from the experience of Canadians in all walks of life from police to clergy to teachers, as my friend from Sault Ste. Marie expressed, that poverty, child abuse, social injustice creates a climate that will invariably lead to crime.
Beyond that, we provide no services at the community level to isolate the particular cases at an early age that will lead to a "life of crime". We provide no services when first the signs and symptoms of social dislocation and difficulty appear. The services in regard to parental alcoholism are abysmal in this country. Family counselling, adequate housing, proper community development programs at the grass roots level, good community
May 30, 1990

policing, are all hit and miss programs. This country and the government has consistently and persistently failed to address these issues.
As a result, invariably young people even by age six, seven and eight are beginning to show the signs of the pain and agony in their lives which eventually is expressed in violence against others in society.
Then we get to the time when the crimes of the young people become so serious that they come to the attention of the police and the police are left with no services and no system for responding and for heading off the increased problem.
We come to the situation where the criminal justice system, a system which the last Parliament invented, makes the problem even worse. We have the evidence of those who have been working with the Young Offenders Act over the last number of years that we have ended up with even more young people in custody.
The objective of the act was to reduce the number of people in custody in order that we could, hopefully, divert young people from more serious crimes and create a safer and more secure society. Now we have shifted to the point where there has been, after the first five years of life of the Young Offenders Act, even more young people in our jails, even more young people into those schools of crime, which is something no one in this country wants to see. The government, when pressed with the evidence of the complete failure of its work, tries to patch together a minimal solution.
There is one virtue in the bill before the House, but it does not proceed nearly far enough. The virtue is that it makes it slightly easier for a judge to conclude that he or she should keep the young offender in the young offender system rather than transfer the young offender to adult court when it comes to a very serious crime.
Under the Young Offenders Act as it is presently set up, a judge would be faced with a decision; a minimum sentence which he sees as too short, but if he agrees to the transfer to adult court, he is then faced with a sentence which he sees as too long, that is, a minimum 25-year sentence.
Government Orders
The flexibility that our system generally provides judges to come up with a punishment that not only fits the crime, but fits the circumstances of society and of the individual young offender is not in the law as it now stands. The one virtue of this bill is that it increases the minimum sentence from three to five years and reduces for young offenders transferred to adult court the minimum down to ten years.
As I suggest, the bill simply does not go far enough, nor does it deal in any comprehensive way with the real problems. It does not offer any leadership in this area. It has led me to wonder sometimes whether the problem is as much with the government directly or with the advice it is getting from the Department of Justice. Within the narrow scope of the government's particular response, the bill does deal with some of the issues. But the larger mandate given to the Department of Justice for coming up with a response to the rising incidence of young crime in this country is a complete, abject and utter failure, and nothing is more clear about the failure than the government's bill that is now before the House.
As has already been noted, the bill is opposed by organizations from across the country. None are more thorough and precise in this area than the Canadian Council on Children and Youth. This organization has prepared a paper which is 26 pages in length. I will not bore the House by reading the full 26 pages, but let me at least read the conclusion which states:
-dispositional patterns in the youth courts must be carefully monitored. Of particular concern has been the increase in the use of custody and the apparent disparities in dispositional practices. It may in the future be necessary to consider further substantive legislative changes, or amendments to the Act's Declaration of Principle or the creation of sentencing guidelines, in order to ensure that custody is not used inappropriately or excessively.
More fundamentally, it must be appreciated that the law is a blunt social tool, and can only have a limited effect on a complex problem like youthful criminality. The public is understandably concerned about the issue of violence, in particular among young persons. However, legislation, or changes to legislation, can only have a limited impact on offence patterns of adolescents.
Significant changes in offence patterns are likely to require significant social changes. There have to be improvements in our youth corrections system as well. This is largely a provincial responsibility but the federal government can play a role.
More fundamentally, our mental health, education and welfare systems must be made more responsive to the needs of youth; we need improvements in how we deal with such problems as drug and alcohol

May 30, 1990
Government Orders
abuse, adolescents with learning disabilities, and visible minority
youth, and with the integration of young persons into the labour force.
Most basically, we must have a society that values its youth and
recognizes their need for a nurturing environment.
Anyone who has spent any time in association with the criminal justice system and reviewing the working of the criminal justice system in the countiy will know that, once a young person has found himself or herself within the criminal justice system before the courts under the Young Offenders Act, the system has already failed.
We also know that once a young person is before the young offenders system, nothing in the legislation we already have will help, and nothing in the bill before the House will remedy the deficiencies in the act.
It is important that this bill go back for further consideration; that the House take a comprehensive look at the problems of youthful crime; and that, instead of offering further despair, we begin to offer the leadership of hope so that finally the pain of crime in this area can be eradicated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions or comments, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my seat-mate. It is indeed an honour to sit beside him when he can come up with that kind of factual, practical, sensible, and yet emotional oratory.
He talked about societal problems. Again, I refer to my own setting in school. As a principal of an elementary school for the last 10 years or so, I spent most of my time, unashamedly so, in counselling. I do not use the term "guidance counsellor" because that always connotes preparing people for their vocation in life. The counselling was to assist young people in adjusting to the life-style they were dealt which in many, many cases was very difficult.
My hon. friend used the word "preventative" on at least one occasion. I want to use it several times. We use the word "prevention" in medicine and say that it will save us money. If we expend funds in fire prevention, that will decrease the cost of actually fighting fires. We talk about dental hygiene and the prevention of tooth
decay. Even the dentists who can profit from bad teeth support this.
Yet, one has to wonder why we do not spend more money in crime prevention. It seems to be a very sensible and practical way of dealing with a very serious problem. Could the member elaborate on that concept of expending more funds before rather than after which, in fact, would be cost-saving?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question. It is interesting for me particularly, because in the City of Victoria we have a program which has been noted right across the country in this precise area. That is a community policing program.
The City of Victoria Police Department, a few years ago, with the assistance of the Solicitor General's department, established a program of neighbourhood police stations which in a way is old hat. It is perhaps what the police used to do very well and it is taking that old idea and readapting into a modem urban setting.
Even in establishing the local police station there was a good deal of community consultation and preparation for that. Community committees were established and the community was asked to participate in the work of the neighbourhood police station. Much of the work was focused on the idea of the prevention of crime. I should add that there is also the need to deal with the prevention of the perception of crime. We now have five neighbourhood police stations in Victoria. So far all of them have appeared to be very successful in not only reducing the incidence of crime in the area, and particularly among young people, but also the perception of crime.
Surveys have shown that older people have the greatest fear that they may be subject to crime, and at the same time the surveys show that it is in fact young people who are the greatest victims of crime. Part of that is because crime in our urban society invariably happens at night, frequently associated with abuse of alcohol and drugs. It is quite a different pattern than one watches on television, and I think many of us get our images of crime as much from television and from the media as we do from the reality.
When one asks the police what is their busiest time of day, they will state that it is between 11 at night and four or five in the morning. Therefore, the work of the prevention of crime begins with the bringing into focus a real understanding of what crime is all about.
May 30, 1990

The government could do so much more than it has done in this area. It has given some support to some work in this area, but persistently when they get around to announcing what they are going to do, they have great press conferences, they produce wonderful books, they announce that the RCMP is going to get some extra people to go around and arrest some more people, and then they come up with flimsy bills like this that do not come close to addressing the heart of the problem, and they have shown no national leadership.
Even in the United States, the federal government has shown greater leadership in trying to develop effective and sensible programs for the prevention of crime. In Britain, if it is possible to imagine it, Margaret Thatcher has shown, finally, some understanding about the causes of crime and has given some assistance to some very good crime prevention programs at the local level.
My colleagues say that they cannot believe it. It is true. At least I am told it is true and my sources are impeccable in this area.
I see there is a minute or two left. I do not know whether my friends from any part of the House have further questions, but I will conclude in time for them to ask them if they do.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for an excellent speech, a very comprehensive speech. I know that many of my colleagues from other parts of the country also want to participate in the debate on this important legislation, and over the coming weeks and months we look forward to having those views expressed on this important legislation.
Government Orders
I wanted to draw to the attention of my colleague the fact that the acting police chief in Edmonton, Alberta, has stated that the changes which are proposed by the government in the area of the Young Offenders Act are only a distraction and will not make a significant impact on the problem of teen crime. My colleague referred to the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and I wanted to draw to his attention the fact that at least one chief of police has said that this bill is not the way to go, that instead we should be looking at more counselling and more preventive programs.
I am pleased to draw that to the attention of my colleague and also to note the fine work that has been done in the city of Victoria in the area of crime prevention, as well as in the municipality of Burnaby which has an excellent young offenders advisory group. Under the progressive leadership of Mayor Copeland and the council there, and the progressive leadership of the mayor of Victoria, certainly we can do a great deal in the area of crime prevention, particularly involving young people.
I see it is six o'clock and I will draw my remarks to a close.
